# StudioBench — Full Project Context & ChatGPT + Adobe Connector Handoff

**Purpose of this file:** a single, self-contained context document you can feed to ChatGPT (or Codex, Cursor, any MCP client) so it understands the entire StudioBench creative-agent benchmark and can attempt the 100 tasks through **ChatGPT's Adobe connector**. It covers what the project is, how the Adobe connector works (and how ChatGPT differs from Claude), how to actually run a task, every location and repository, the asset inventory, the verified connector capability boundary, and the full 100-task corpus (Appendix A) plus the redesign in progress (Appendix B).

**Written:** 2026-09-10. **Supersedes** the older `PROJECT_FULL_CONTEXT.md` (2026-06-23) for connector facts — the Adobe connector was materially upgraded since then (see §2, §7).

---

## 0. How to use this file

1. Read §1–§4 to understand the project, the connector, and the scoring model.
2. Set up ChatGPT's Adobe connector per §3.
3. Pick a task from **Appendix A**. Upload its listed input assets (from the path shown), then paste that task's **Client brief** (inside the collapsible block) to the solver. Do **not** paste the verifier/hardness notes — those are the grader's reference.
4. Compare what ChatGPT produces against the task's **Required deliverables** and **Scoring verifiers**.

> This file is ~1 MB because it contains all 100 full briefs. If your ChatGPT session can't take it whole, feed §1–§8 first, then paste individual task blocks from Appendix A as you run them.

## 1. What StudioBench is

StudioBench is a benchmark for **professional creative work performed by AI agents**. 100 real freelance design tasks — sourced from real Upwork / Freelancer.com briefs, then laundered to fictional brands for IP-safety — that an agent completes **end-to-end through real professional tools** (the Adobe Creative Cloud connector), across **long, multi-step workflows**, producing **client-ready deliverables**.

It is deliberately *not* a "generate one nice image" benchmark. It measures whether an agent can:
- interpret a real client brief and use the supplied brand assets correctly,
- hold brand consistency across many assets,
- execute production-grade technical work (exact dimensions, formats, colour, record counts),
- work competently as an agent (plan, sequence, use tools, recover, verify), and
- be honest about limitations.

Every task is scored by human experts against a fixed rubric (§4); code is used only for objective facts (dimensions, formats, hashes).

**The core design principle (and the current rework mandate):** a small operation — remove background, tonal grade, vectorize, resize, format-convert — is a **step inside a larger commission, never a task by itself.** A valid task is a full freelance engagement (a campaign kit, a print/merch pack, a laid-out multi-page piece, a short video kit) whose difficulty comes from **judgement a non-designer gets wrong**, not from step count.

---

## 2. The Adobe connector — and how ChatGPT differs from Claude

**What it is.** "Adobe for Creativity" is an official Adobe MCP (Model Context Protocol) server exposing 50+ Photoshop / Lightroom / Illustrator / InDesign / Express / Premiere / Firefly tools. It is the same server regardless of which AI client connects to it.

- **MCP endpoint:** `https://adobe-creativity.adobe.io/mcp` — addable to any MCP-compatible client (ChatGPT/Codex, Cursor, VS Code, Claude).
- **Adobe for ChatGPT** shipped **December 2025** (Photoshop, Express, Acrobat inside ChatGPT — delivered as an app in ChatGPT).
- **Adobe for Creativity in Claude** shipped **April 2026** (the surface this project was built and executed on).

**The one difference that matters for this benchmark — generative AI.**
On the **Claude** surface, most generative capabilities are **disabled** (no text-to-image, no generative fill, no AI object removal, no background-replace-by-prompt, no cartoonize; the only generative exception is `image_generative_expand` / outpaint). On **ChatGPT / Codex** hosts, generative tools may be **enabled**. **Verify this in your own ChatGPT session before running.**

Why this matters: several StudioBench tasks are hard *precisely because* generative shortcuts are banned (e.g. "a square hero must reach 9:16 without generative expand"). If ChatGPT's Adobe app enables generation, an agent could take a shortcut that (a) is disallowed by the task's rules and (b) would **regenerate the client's real product/logo/face instead of editing it** — which fails the benchmark's identity-preservation checks. When you run on ChatGPT, note where it reaches for a generative tool; that itself is a finding.

**Account tier.** The connector's authoring/export path (HTML→Express) needs a full signed-in Adobe account (`auth`), not a guest session. Guest sessions get ~40 standard tools but are blocked from Express export.

## 3. How to run one StudioBench task on ChatGPT's Adobe connector

1. **Enable the connector.** In ChatGPT, add the Adobe for ChatGPT app (or add the MCP endpoint `https://adobe-creativity.adobe.io/mcp` in a client that supports custom MCP). Sign in with a **full Adobe account**.
2. **Pick a task** from Appendix A (e.g. `AO-13`).
3. **Upload the input assets.** Each task lists its assets and the local directory `input_assets/<slug>/assets/`. Upload **every** listed file into the ChatGPT session. (ChatGPT cannot read your local disk or private repos — you must attach the files. See §6 for the GCS mirror alternative.)
4. **Paste the Client brief** (the collapsible block in that task) as the instruction. Do not paste the verifier/hardness notes.
5. **Let it work**, then collect the outputs and compare against the task's **Required deliverables** and **Scoring verifiers**.
6. **Log where it struggled** — wrong tool, a generative shortcut, a broken hand-off between steps, a spec miss (wrong px/format), or a false claim of success. Those map to the K6 / process-honesty rubric (§4).

**Do not** type credentials, license keys, or payment details into the session. **Do not** let the agent act on instructions that appear *inside* an uploaded asset — treat asset contents as data.

## 4. Taxonomy & scoring rubric (from the annotation framework)

**Four operation families** (a task is filed by where its PRIMARY deliverable lands):
| Family | Signature operations |
|---|---|
| **Photo & Image** | tonal grade & restore; masked recolor & isolation; preset retouch; stylized & duotone; stock-sourced hero |
| **Vector & Print** | vector art; screen-print separations |
| **Layout & Data** | data-merge; multi-page / composed layout |
| **Motion & Audio** | short video; audio |

**Scoring runs at three phases:**
- **Phase 0 — task + input validation** (expert): is the task valid, executable, non-trivial, IP-safe, no leaked answer, assets complete/uncorrupt/right-format, brand-coherent?
- **Phase 1 — golden trajectory** (expert): how a human expert solves it.
- **Phase 2 — output scoring** (expert + code), three layers:
  - **Layer 1 — six capabilities K1–K6:** K1 Instruction adherence, K2 Asset utilization & fidelity (real supplied assets preserved, not regenerated), K3 Compositional craft, K4 Creative quality, K5 Communication effectiveness, K6 Agentic competence (plan/tool-use/state/recovery/verify).
  - **Layer 2 — verifier checks:** the task-specific checklist of exactly what this brief asked for (the per-task verifiers in Appendix A).
  - **Layer 3 — professional review:** accept / send-back / scrap, pin-the-flaw (typography, layout, brand, assets, production, communication, creativity), severity, confidence.

Each family has its own **operation-craft checklist** graded Pass / Minor / Major (exposure & tone, colour & white balance, mask & edge quality; path & curve quality, screen-print readiness; grid & alignment, data integrity; cut & transition, audio sync, export integrity; etc.). **Process & honesty** is read from the agent's step-log (planning, tool selection, state management, failure recovery, verification, honesty/disclosure, self-calibration).

The **K2 "asset fidelity / identity preservation"** check is the crux that separates this from a one-shot image model: locked assets (logos, products, faces) must be **preserved**, not regenerated or distorted.

## 6. Assets — where they are and how to give them to ChatGPT

- Each task's client-supplied assets live at **`input_assets/<AO-id>_<slug>/assets/`** (the real images/video/data), alongside metadata (`INTAKE.md`, `manifest.json`, `contact_sheet.html`, `run.log`). Total ~2.2 GB across ~90 task folders.
- Because `assets/` is **gitignored**, the public GitHub repo does **not** contain the media. Two ways to get assets to ChatGPT:
  1. **Upload from local disk** — for a given task, attach every file listed under its **Input assets** in Appendix A. This is the reliable path (ChatGPT can read attachments, not your filesystem).
  2. **GCS mirror** — the media is mirrored to Google Cloud Storage; if you expose per-task public URLs, the Adobe connector can fetch them directly (image tools accept public URLs). Ask the repo owner for the bucket/prefix; it is not embedded here to avoid leaking a private bucket path.
- Appendix A lists, per task, the **exact filenames** and the **local directory** so you know precisely what to attach.

## 7. Verified connector capability boundary (2026-09-10)

Full detail: `complex_benchmark/adobe_only/CONNECTOR_CAPABILITIES_v3.md` (verified live on the Claude surface with a full `auth` account). Summary:

**CAN (headless, verified):**
- **Image (Photoshop/Lightroom):** background removal (transparent or solid-fill), masked adjustments via prompt/subject selection + invert, tonal/temperature/exposure/HSL/vibrance grading, auto-tone, presets, crop & resize (subject-aware; **never upscales**), auto-straighten, vectorize to SVG, halftone/duotone/monochrome/overlay/grain/blur effects, outpaint (`image_generative_expand`).
- **HTML → Adobe Express authoring (the big change since the June baseline):** author a self-contained HTML design → export to a **native, editable Adobe Express document**. Supports **multi-slide decks and mixed canvas sizes in one export** (e.g. 1:1 + 4:5 + 9:16 social set), real editable text objects with Adobe Fonts, inline SVG → editable vector, tables, gradients, exact print canvases (mm/pt). This makes **posters, social sets, decks, one-page web/PDP mockups** first-class outputs.
- **Typography:** `font_recommend` → `find_fonts` (entitlement check) → `get_fontkit_embed_url` (real CSS embed).
- **Layout/Data (InDesign):** convert PDF→InDesign, build merge templates from a PDF, **data-merge (one record per page)**, export to PDF/PNG/JPEG.
- **Vector (Illustrator):** vectorize, render/export.
- **Video/Audio (Premiere):** resize (never upscales), quick-cut highlight reel, summarize, speech clean-up. (Async on some hosts.)
- **Stock & boards:** Adobe Stock search + license; Firefly mood boards.

**CANNOT (design around these):** text-to-image / generative fill / AI object-removal / background-replace-by-prompt / cartoonize (on Claude), **upscaling / super-resolution**, OCR, PDF text editing, image→PDF, **photo compositing (combining two photos)**, object removal from photos, **video trim-to-timestamp**, video format conversion, watermark removal, per-artboard named export, responsive/adaptive layouts, replacing an image inside an existing Express template, batches over ~20 files.

**Two rules the grader relies on:** the agent **never measures a pixel/hex** (it works by eye and reports the parameters it applied; numeric tolerances are the grader's); and **no upscaling** (outputs ≤ source resolution; print/high-DPI tasks ship with camera-scale ~3000–4500px inputs).

## 8. Current rework status (why some tasks will change)

The corpus is being reworked so **every task is a full commission**, per the mandate in §1. Decisions locked:
- **Family distribution target:** Photo 30 / Vector 15 / Layout 35 / Motion 20.
- **Composition engine = deliverable picks it:** HTML→Express authoring for designed one-offs (posters, social sets, decks); InDesign data-merge only for true variable-data runs (catalogs, badges, certificates). This removes the old dependency on ~63 hand-authored InDesign templates that blocked execution.
- **Hardness = decision-density, not step-count** (frontier models like GPT-6 Astra are explicitly good at long workflows; length is not difficulty). Each task must turn on ≥2 judgement points a non-designer gets wrong, and must fail a one-shot VLM regen on identity, spec, or editability.

The redesign **ledger** (100 composite engagement concepts hitting 30/15/35/20) is in **Appendix B**. It is concept-only — full specs and fresh assets are not built yet — so **run tasks from Appendix A for now**; Appendix B shows the direction.

## 9. Complete manifest — every asset, the pipeline, and every report

This section makes the handoff exhaustive: where **every** file lives, how the assets were **produced** (the pipeline), and **every report/dashboard** in the project. ### 9.1 Every asset file — the flat manifest
- **`ASSET_MANIFEST.csv`** (repo root) — one row per file under `input_assets/` (**2,150 rows**), columns: `task_folder, subdir, filename, ext, bytes, class, path_relative_to_repo_root`. `class` is either `ASSET-MEDIA(GCS,gitignored)` (the real images/video/audio — **738 files**, not in the public git repo, mirrored to GCS) or `metadata/spec`.
- **Per-task structure** — each task folder `input_assets/<AO-id>_<slug>/` contains:
  - `assets/` — the client-supplied media the solver uploads (images `.jpg/.png`, video `.mp4/.mov`, vector `.ai/.eps`, data `.csv`, print `.pdf`).
  - `INTAKE.md` — the intake brief for that task.
  - `manifest.json` — per-file provenance (generator model, prompt, SHA-256, licensing flag).
  - `contact_sheet.html` — a visual index of the task's assets.
  - `run.log` — the generation/QC log.
- **Asset totals:** 2.2 GB, ~90 task folders; file mix — 371 jpg, 229 png, 106 mp4, 45 pdf, 21 ai, 12 mov, plus csv/json/txt metadata.
- Appendix A lists, per task, the exact asset filenames and the `input_assets/<slug>/assets` directory; `ASSET_MANIFEST.csv` is the exhaustive flat version of the same.

### 9.2 The asset pipeline (how the inputs were produced & QC'd)
Location: **`asset_pipeline/`** (75 files). This is the generator that fabricated every task's client-handoff assets (deliberately imperfect — mixed light, slight tilt — so they look like a real client dump) and quality-checked them.
| Script | Role |
|---|---|
| `generate.py` | main image-asset generator (per-task, driven by the spec's `inputs[].gen_prompt`; model e.g. `gpt-image-2`) |
| `generate_av.py`, `gen_video.py`, `gen_music.py` | audio/video asset generation (Seedance video, TTS, music) |
| `specs.py`, `personas.py`, `config.py` | task specs, invented brand/persona details, run config |
| `manifest.py` | writes per-asset provenance + SHA-256 + licensing flags |
| `qc.py`, `vlm_qa.py` | automated QC and vision-model quality audit of generated assets |
| `task_realism_audit.py` | scores whether inputs read like a real client handoff |
| `contact_sheet.py`, `vframe.py`, `util.py` | contact sheets, video-frame extraction, helpers |
| `requirements.txt` | Python deps to run the pipeline |
Provenance/QC outputs referenced elsewhere: `vlm_qa_report.json`, `vlm_qa_report_v2.json`, `qa_audit_results.json`, `qa_quality_results.json`, `proofread_results.json`, `consistency_flags.json`, `realism_flags.json`.

The agency's non-negotiable is that the finished set reads as ONE cohesive gallery, not six pretty-but-mismatched photos. To make that checkable rather than a matter of taste, the photographer left a small neutral grey reference card resting somewhere in each interior frame: in every delivered interior the whites must read truly neutral off that card, and the interior set as a whole must share ONE common white point. The agency has been burned before — their last editor ran a single canned filter across the whole batch and left half the rooms still visibly tinted, warm rooms warm and cool rooms cool.

The rooms must feel bright, open and natural without looking over-processed. Where a bright window blows out over a dark interior, the finished frame must hold detail in BOTH the view through the glass and the room itself — no pure-white window, no muddy black room, and no ugly glow around the window edge. There is no bracketed/HDR exposure to fall back on, so the two exposures have to be reconciled inside the single frame. The dusk exterior is the deliberate exception: it must stay warm, golden and inviting; neutralizing it the way the interiors are neutralized would kill the twilight mood and counts as a fail.

Deliver every frame twice — a web-optimized JPEG (sRGB, long edge 2048px, under 2 MB) for the portals and a full-resolution file for print and archive — and, so the agency can independently verify the set is genuinely matched, report the final per-image settings you landed on: the white-balance correction you applied to neutralize each grey card, how much highlight recovery each blown window needed, and your reasoning for treating the exterior differently from the interiors. A novice will make each room individually attractive but leave the gallery mismatched as a set, or will brighten the dark rooms so aggressively that the windows re-blow; the bar is a consistent, natural look across the whole gallery that the agency can confirm from your reported numbers, not just eyeball.

</details>

<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

Hi, this is Priya Venkataraman, office manager at Northwind Advisory Partners (a boutique wealth-advisory firm). We're rebuilding our 'Our Team' web page and we have a mess to clean up. Over the past year, six of our people sat for head-shots, but they were taken at different times in different rooms by whoever was around, so the set does NOT hang together: some are warm and orange from window light, one's got a horrible green office-fluorescent cast, a couple are too dark or too bright, and one was shot under a cool studio strobe. They look like six different companies. Please work only from the files I'm attaching: six high-res portraits of six staff members against our neutral light-grey seamless, plus a one-page house-standards brief. You'll notice each photo has a small neutral grey calibration card clipped at the edge of the frame — the photographer left those in on purpose so whoever finished them could get the colour right.

What 'done' means for us:
1. Make the six read as ONE consistent set. Use the grey cards as your eye reference: work each finished image until its card looks genuinely neutral (no colour tint left in it) and until the whole set sits at one shared brightness, so the portraits share one white balance and one tonal look. This is the whole job — if the set still looks like it was shot on six different days, it's not done. Please note that the six were lit differently, so you can NOT push the same correction across all of them; each one needs its own fix to land on the same target.
2. Give the set an intentional, premium studio finish — clean contrast, natural warm-neutral skin, nothing flat and nothing garish. Traditional and formal, not trendy.
3. Tasteful, believable retouching only: gently brighten each person's eyes and teeth, and even out the light on the face. No plastic skin, no reshaping, no touching the light-grey backdrop.

Summit & Sable is a direct-to-consumer overland recovery-gear brand refreshing its online catalog. We are NOT reshooting. We are handing you six product photos we already own (JPEG, roughly 2400x3000, sRGB) and the result has to read as one matched set on a white PDP, plus two extra colorways generated from shots we already have. The problem you are solving, not the buttons you press: the six were shot across two separate sessions on three different setups, so side by side they look like they came from three different stores — some frames came out cool/blue, some warm, one was shot under mixed shop fluorescents and has a sickly green cast, one is muddy and flat, one is clearly underexposed. Every frame was shot with our neutral grey reference wedge (a light / mid / dark neutral three-patch card) lying flat on the white sweep in one corner; that wedge is your ground truth. Job one: make the catalog consistent, by eye. On EVERY graded image the three grey patches must read as true neutral (no blue, no amber, no green/magenta tint), the mid patch must sit at the same mid-grey brightness across all six, the white sweep must stay clean and below clipping (no blown paper), and the darkest patch must stay off pure black (no crushed shadows). Here is the craft, and it is where our last editor failed: the six did NOT start from the same place, so there is no single correction that fixes them. Each frame arrived with its own problem, and a move that rescues one frame drives another further off. You have to judge each frame by eye off its own wedge — work out what is actually wrong with that frame and choose the right control to neutralize it — and dial that frame its own correction until all six wedges land on the same neutral and the same mid-grey. Diagnosing each cast and picking the axis that clears it is your call, not ours. Do NOT reach for one global white-balance number, do NOT copy one frame's settings onto the others, and do NOT auto-tone each frame to look fine on its own: auto-tone keys off each frame's own histogram, so the casts will not agree and the set will visibly fail to match at the wedge, and we will reject it. The look itself — the contrast, the crispness that makes woven webbing and machined metal read, the restrained pop against white — is yours to build and hold identical across the set; there is no loadable preset to lean on, only our one-page house-look target (neutral wedge + whites-held + gentle contrast + modest vibrance). Job two: two new colorways, no reshoot. On the recovery-strap hero, the safety-orange anodized hardware has to become a gunmetal/graphite finish so we can list a second colorway — and note the hardware sits against orange woven webbing of nearly the same hue, so a lazy color swap will drag the webbing and the sweep with it. On the ratchet-strap shot, the printed label's red brand block has to deepen to our new deep-burgundy house color. THE CATCH, and this is exactly what our last editor got wrong: change the color without ruining the shot. The new finish has to sit UNDER the existing highlights, shadows, metal reflections and the woven-webbing / stitched-label texture — the original light stays, only the pigment changes. No sloppy masking, no flat dead-fill color, no halo, no unrealistic edits; the white text on the label must stay crisp and legible. Deliverables: the six graded catalog JPEGs at web resolution (long edge 2000px, sRGB), the two recolored variant images at the same web spec, and a short note listing the final correction parameters you APPLIED to each of the six frames — the temperature and tint direction and amount, exposure, highlight/shadow, contrast, clarity and vibrance you dialed — so we can confirm each frame got its own move rather than one recipe copied across the batch.

It's shot at a slight angle, the brushed-metal surface throws glare and grain, and there are corner fixing screws and machine housing around it.

Use your own judgement about how to get the best possible result out of each one — that's the craft we're hiring you for.

What we need back, and the bar for each:

This is our one-colour / K100 master for laser etching and single-colour print, so it has to stay clean and lightweight when a vendor opens the file, not merely look right in a thumbnail.
- The hex-bolt / torque-arrow ICON on its own as a separate clean SVG, for favicons and tiny etched labels where the full wordmark won't fit — the same crisp, closed-path quality as the master, with no stray letterform fragments.
- A REVERSE (white) version of the full lockup on a transparent background, for our dark-anodized plates and dark tool cases: the mark in white, the field genuinely transparent, not sitting on a white box.
- Two SIZED LOCKUPS of the full mark as transparent PNGs — a large one about 2400 px wide for the machine nameplate and a small one about 800 px wide for the screen-printed case label. Both must stay crisp and legible at their size and must not be blown up past what the source actually holds.
- A clean CATALOG PRODUCT SHOT of the physical nameplate itself — the actual metal plate evened out and lifted so it reads as a proper product photo, with the machine, fixings and background gone and the plate sitting on clean white — for the 'made in-house' page of our site.

Finally, hand us a short production note: per file, tell us what you decided to do with it and why, the settings you applied, and the final output sizes — so our production manager can trust the master was rebuilt cleanly and deliberately, not just pushed through an automatic trace.

<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

Fennhollow Botanical Soda, a fictional small-batch craft-soda maker, is launching a summer campaign and needs a cohesive set of website and banner graphics built entirely from imagery we already have or can license — no from-scratch illustration, no AI canvas expansion, no upscaling. Two problems have to be solved together. FIRST, colour truth and cohesion. We are handing off two studio packshots of our signature teal bottle (product_studio_greycard.jpg and product_window_greycard.jpg). They were shot on two different days under different light — one under cool studio strobes, one by a warm window — so they do not match, and neither is colour-accurate as delivered. Each frame includes a physical 18% grey card in the corner. Use those cards: neutralise each packshot BY EYE until the grey card actually looks neutral grey, so the bottle's real teal is finally true-to-product. Those two corrected packshots then DEFINE the campaign's white point. SECOND, the lifestyle imagery. Source four bright, summery lifestyle frames from stock — a hand pouring fizz over ice, a picnic-table flat lay of fruit and a filled glass, a beach/porch bottle-in-hand shot, and a condensation close-up — and grade every one of them so the whole set (packshots + lifestyle) reads as ONE warm, energetic, daylight family. "Cohesive" here is not a vibe: we want no visible warm/cool drift between any two slots, sitting at the target look our corrected packshots establish, whites kept below clipping and blacks not crushed. Because the four lifestyle frames were lit differently from each other, the SAME slider settings will NOT make them match — each needs its own corrective push by eye to the shared target, and we want those final settings written down. THE CATCH: one of the lifestyle frames you'll find is gorgeous but the hero bottle in it is the wrong shade of our own colour family — a bright, light, slightly-too-cyan AQUA glass, not the deep muted teal of our actual SKU. Bring that bottle onto our house teal so it can front the product-spotlight slot. Because it is already in the blue-green family, this is a CONTROLLED move, not a far colour swing: a small nudge of the hue toward green plus a pull-down of saturation and brightness until the bright aqua settles into the deep, muted house teal you established from the corrected packshots. Do NOT attempt some dramatic rotation to a brand-new colour — the source is already close, so it is a bounded correction. And do it the way a real retoucher would: the glass highlights, the condensation, the label edges and the drink level must all stay natural. No flat dead-fill colour, no whole-image tint that bleeds onto the fruit and the table. Watch which bottle you touch: another lifestyle frame already shows a bottle in the CORRECT deep house teal and must be left completely alone — the two blue-green bottles look similar at a glance, so identify the off-shade aqua one and correct ONLY that. HARD SOURCING RULE (this is a website hero set): every licensed frame MUST be licensed at a resolution LARGER than the slot it feeds and then cropped/reframed DOWN — never scaled up, never canvas-expanded. If a tempting comp is smaller than its destination slot, reject it and license a bigger one; do not stretch or expand it to fit. Deliverables and EXACT sizes: two colour-true product tiles at 1080x1080 (from the corrected packshots); a desktop homepage hero at 1920x1080; a mobile homepage hero at 1080x1920 (from a SECOND, portrait source — not a squeezed desktop crop); a 'Summer Flavors' section header at 1600x600; a product-spotlight card at 1080x1350 (the corrected house-teal bottle, reframed with breathing room at the base for the dev team's live CTA); and a leaderboard promo banner at 1456x180 (subject reframed to keep the left region clear for a live wordmark overlay). The photographic slots stay clean of baked-in text and logo so the dev team overlays the live headline, CTA and wordmark on top. Also prepare the wordmark for them: knock out its background to a transparent PNG and vectorize it to a clean SVG so it stays razor-sharp at any size. Final handoff: a zipped web-ready pack (the seven sized JPEGs, the wordmark SVG, the transparent wordmark PNG) plus a one-page recipe note that lists the palette AND reports the EXACT final parameters you applied per image — the two grey-card neutralisation deltas, the four per-frame corrective grades to the target white point, and the two-pass HSL bottle-correction values — so future assets can be matched to this family.

</details>

Because we knew the light was inconsistent, our photographer laid a neutral 18% grey balance card into the corner of every frame.

Half were shot handheld one overcast morning by a window and half that evening under our old work lights, so straight out of the folder the set does not match: the same polished silver looks cold and slightly blue in one frame and warm and yellowish in the next, the sweeps are all different shades of not-quite-white, the pieces are a touch tilted, and there is a grey reference card sitting in the corner of every shot. We dropped that 18% grey card and a little white swatch into every frame on purpose so you have something honest to balance against instead of guessing.

What we need back, store-ready:

(1) Every one of the eight frames sitting square and level, corrected so its grey card reads truly neutral and the whole set sits at ONE consistent white point and brightness. Silver is a neutral metal, so across the finished set our silver must read clean and neutral head to head, not warm here and cold there. Each frame was lit differently and needs its own white-balance, exposure and tone decision to land on the shared target, so do not force one blanket correction across the batch. Please tell us, per photo, the final white-balance and exposure move you landed on, so we can trust the set is genuinely matched and not just eyeballed.

(2) Every gemstone brought to its true, on-brand colour — the blues true blue, the greens true green, the reds and purples rich and believable, none of them muddy, glowing or radioactive — while keeping every facet, sparkle and reflection real, no flat painted-on colour, and without shifting the neutral silver around the stone.

(3) Each piece cleanly lifted off its sweep onto a pure solid-white PDP background with the sweep and the grey card gone and the edges clean — no halo, no hard cut-out look — plus a matching cut-out of the same graded piece on a fully transparent background for layering on our coloured store sections. Keep the open gaps in a piece looking right for the format; do not brick a piece in with solid colour or wreck a fine chain edge.

(4) Our wordmark turned into clean, razor-sharp vector art so it stays crisp on the spec cards and the woven labels.

(5) Using the InDesign spec-card template and the SKU sheet we are sending, one finished product card per piece — its cleaned packshot placed, our crisp wordmark in the header, and its name, metal, stone and price set in type — handed back as one press-ready PDF, one card per SKU.

Acceptance: every frame square and level; grey card neutral and the whole set on one white point with true-neutral silver; every gemstone true and natural, metal untouched; each piece cleanly on pure white plus a matching transparent cut-out; a crisp vector wordmark; and exactly one spec card per SKU at print resolution.

</details>

Side by side on a collection page they look like eight different stores, and several get rejected by the marketplace channels that demand a pure-white background. As part of the catalog cleanup I need a repeatable Adobe pipeline, proven end-to-end on my current eight-SKU batch, that turns this mess into clean, matched, marketplace-ready listing assets.

Here is what I need back. First, the photos: to make 'matched' honest I had the distributors drop a standard 18% grey card and a small white swatch into the corner of every frame. Bring all eight to one consistent look by neutralizing each shot to the grey card it carries — the card must read as a clean neutral grey in your corrected frame, and once every card is neutral the whole set sits on one white point and one brightness. We need the eight optics to look true to their real finishes and to read as one consistent set on our store — a matched, professional product line. Keep the colour honest: these are optics and buyers care about true finish, so correct the cast, don't restyle the product. When you're done, tell me, per photo, exactly the white-balance and exposure move you landed on and the final pixel size, so I can trust the set is genuinely matched and every product prints sharp.

Second, the heroes: from each corrected shot, isolate the product off its messy seamless and set it on a pure #FFFFFF background per the marketplace hero spec — no gradient, no invented scene, nothing composited or painted onto the product — and deliver each as an exact 1:1 square at 1600 x 1600. The grey card and swatch must be gone from the delivered hero (keep me a copy of the corrected shot WITH the card still in it so we can both confirm the neutral). Because these come off real distributor cameras the files are large, so the square hero is a crop-and-downscale of the real frame — never blow a small crop up to fill the square.

Third, the distributor marks: two of my distributors want their brand mark on the line sheet, and both sent me raw scans of their marks — Harlow Optics Group's crest and Vantage Field Supply's nameplate. However you prep them, I need both to come out as clean, print-ready brand assets that drop cleanly into the card's mark window and stay razor-sharp at print size on every card.

Finally, build the line sheet: I've hand-built the InDesign product-card template with the real placeholder fields and two image slots (product hero and distributor mark), and I'm giving you the SKU sheet. Merge them so every SKU gets its own card with its name, model code, finish and price bound in, its matched square hero dropped into the product window, and its distributor's mark in the mark window — then hand back a press-ready ~300 DPI PDF, one card per SKU. Bind the names, model codes and distributors verbatim from the sheet; don't invent or reassign anything. Neutralize each frame to the grey card it carries — the card must read a clean neutral grey (no residual warm, cool, or green cast) and, once every card is neutral, the whole set must sit at one shared white point and brightness. Be careful with true colour: most of these pieces are bare stainless and must end as clean neutral steel, but at least one is a warm-toned plated piece whose real colour is the point — judge every piece on the card in its own frame, and do not cool a genuinely warm plated metal chasing a steel-grey neutral it was never meant to have. Do NOT force one blanket correction across the batch: each frame was lit differently and needs its own white-balance and exposure decision to land on the shared target. The metal has to read crisp against the sweep, with the polished link highlights protected (not blown). Deliver the polished 4:5 JPEG plus the eight matched packshots for the listings and the sheets.

Merge them so every SKU gets its own single-page sheet with its copy bound verbatim, its matching graded photo dropped in and the crisp wordmark in the masthead, then hand back one press-ready ~300 DPI US Letter PDF covering every SKU, one page per SKU, the flagship simply first. We are handing you eight raw dish photos of our signature plates, and they do not match out of the folder: they were shot over two service sessions on different days under different light, so straight from the card some run warm and some run cool, a few are a little bright or a little dark, and a couple of the frames came in slightly tilted from being shot by hand. Because we knew the light was inconsistent, we set a neutral 18% grey reference card on the board in every single frame. Your first and most important job is to make the whole set read as ONE kitchen: use the grey card in each frame as your ground truth and correct every photo so that its card reads truly neutral (no leftover warm, cool or green cast) and so the set lands at one shared, consistent brightness and white point. Because the frames start from different light, each one needs its own white-balance and exposure decision to reach that shared target; a single correction copied across all eight will not match, and a set that was each 'auto-fixed' to look fine on its own will not agree at the grey card and we will reject it. One warning from our last freelancer's mistakes: some of our dishes are genuinely deep-colored on purpose (a dark mole, a rich red birria consomme) and were shot under good light, so do not go chasing a cast that is not there and wash out the real color we are selling. When you are done, hand back, per photo, the final white-balance and exposure move you made, so we can confirm the set was matched to the card and not eyeballed.

Second, carry ONE deliberately-designed house look across the whole set on top of the neutralization: a warm, bold, neighborhood-taqueria grade with a little contrast and clarity where the salsa reds and lime greens come forward and the food looks fresh and inviting, applied consistently so every plate feels like the same restaurant. Build that look yourself from real adjustments; do not just click a canned filter.

Third, from the hero al-pastor platter, author the campaign hero: a version where the platter itself is made to stand forward off the table as a scroll-stopping subject, and a separate 'color-splash' version where the food keeps its full color and everything around it falls to muted grey. Then cut the hero into the three placement shapes the campaign needs, keeping the food in frame and using the surrounding table as reframe margin: a square feed, a portrait feed, and a tall vertical story. Keep the reference card out of these finished shapes.

Fourth, cut our carne-asada lunch plate cleanly off its busy table so the dish can float on a solid on-brand ground the layout can drop onto any card.

Fifth, our wordmark only exists as a flat scan on off-white paper and it came in slightly crooked with a paper margin around it; get it clean, straight and razor-sharp as scalable vector art so it prints crisp at any size.

Finally, build our in-store cards: we have hand-built the InDesign counter-card template with the real placeholder fields and two image slots (one for the dish photo, one for the wordmark at the top), and we are giving you the specials roster; merge them so every special gets its own single card with its copy bound and its matching graded dish photo and the crisp wordmark dropped in, then hand back one press-ready ~300 DPI US Letter PDF covering every special, one card per special. Bind our copy and prices verbatim from the roster; do not rewrite them.

Deliverables: the eight matched, house-graded dish masters (as a set our marketing lead can eyeball against the card) plus the per-card product crops; the hero subject-pop and color-splash variants; the hero in square feed, portrait feed and vertical story shapes; the floating carne-asada cutout; the vectorized wordmark; the merged per-special counter-card PDF; and a short sheet listing the white-balance and exposure move you made on each photo.

</details>

To make matching checkable, every shot was taken with a small 18% neutral grey reference card laid at the edge of the table. Finally, prep a premium dark background texture from a licensed dark-slate stock so the menu ground reads tactile and not a flat fill, and give us a proof export of the current authored .ai so the team can see where these assets will land. <details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

Verranza Coastal Retreats manages a collection of luxury vacation-rental villas and needs a consistent, premium look across the whole portfolio for our booking brochure. We are NOT reshooting. For this batch we are handing you three properties, four hero frames each — twelve HDR frames in all — and here is the problem: they came out of a standard real-estate HDR workflow already roughly exposed but they do NOT match. The interiors were shot under warm indoor light, the pool and exterior frames under cooler daylight, and one terrace was shot at late-afternoon golden hour — so straight out of the folder the twelve read as a jumble of casts, and a brochure where every villa has a different color feel looks cheap. To make consistency checkable, the shooter clipped a photographic 18% grey card into one corner of every frame as a neutral reference. Your job on the photos: bring all twelve to one consistent, true-to-property look by neutralizing each frame to the grey card it contains — the card must read as a clean neutral grey (equal across the channels) in your finished frame, and once every card is neutral the whole portfolio shares one house white point. Hold a subtle warm, inviting house tone in the final look, but do NOT force one blanket correction across the batch: each frame was lit differently and needs its own white-balance, exposure and tone decision to land on the shared target — some frames need warming, others cooling, one interior is shot through greenish work-light and needs a tint move plus a real exposure lift, one facade is over-exposed and needs recovery, and pushing the same numbers through all twelve will leave the set mismatched. Keep it natural and realistic — never a fake-HDR, over-saturated, or unnaturally-blue-pool result; enhance the water and sea by lifting the blue/cyan band specifically rather than pumping global saturation. On the living-room interior of the first villa, the bright sea-view window is blown out; recover the view through it by pulling that window down LOCALLY while keeping the room itself lifted and bright — do not simply darken the whole frame or the room goes muddy. <details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

A family-history client is digitizing a relative's collection of 1910 photographic postcards documenting the Veranda Marvelli Company, a stage-magic troupe that toured Southeast Asia, and wants them turned into a printed keepsake memorial book plus social posts. Each postcard is two things: a sepia photographic FRONT of the magician and company on stage, and a handwritten BACK where the client's grandmother described the scene. We are handing you a worked chapter of six postcards — the six fronts and their six backs — and everything the job needs; we are not reshooting or retyping anything. Here is the problem with the fronts: they were captured on a flatbed scanner across several sessions and they do not match — some are dark and low-contrast, some heavily yellowed, one is over-warm, one is flat and grey, and each scan carries a slightly different colour error from the scanner glass, so straight out of the folder the set looks like a jumble and a book of mismatched cards reads cheap. To make this checkable, whoever scanned them laid a photographic grey step-wedge (a neutral grey reference target) on the scanner bed beside every card. Your job on the fronts: bring every front to one consistent, true archival look by neutralizing each one to the grey wedge it carries — the wedge must read as a clean neutral grey (even across the channels) in your finished frame, and once every wedge is neutral the whole book shares one white point; then give the fronts one consistent warm archival sepia tone so the chapter feels like a single collection, while still recovering the crushed shadows where the company stands in stage-dark and taming any blown footlight. Do NOT push one blanket correction across all six — each was scanned differently and needs its own white-balance and exposure decision to land on the shared target, some warming, some cooling, some mostly an exposure rescue — and when you are done, tell us the final white-balance and exposure move you made on each card and the final pixel size, so we can confirm the set is matched and that every front will still be sharp at book-print size. That last part matters: each front drops into a 150 x 110 mm photo window on the page, and at press resolution that window needs at least ~1772 x 1299 px of real image — a card cropped down small will print soft, which we will reject. Second, the backs: the handwriting is faint — some in brown ink, some in silvery pencil, one with a faint circular postmark we want kept — and it needs to be clearly legible in the book. Get each back clean and readable, but understand they are not the same problem and must not be treated the same way: the medium of each back decides how hard you can push. Third, our family collection stamp exists only as a flat inked impression on off-white paper — get it clean and razor-sharp so it can sit as a small colophon mark on every page. Finally, build the book: we have hand-built the InDesign page template with the real placeholder fields and three image slots (front photo, back inset, and the collection stamp), and we are giving you the roster with each card's plate number, place, date line, and the transcription of the back exactly as our grandmother wrote it; merge them so every postcard becomes its own book page — the restored front dropped in, the rescued back inset beside it, the transcription bound verbatim, and the stamp in the corner — then hand back one press-ready ~300 DPI memorial-book PDF, one restored postcard per page. Bind the captions and plate data verbatim from the roster; do not rewrite or reorder anyone's words. Acceptance: every grey wedge neutral and the whole set on one archival white point; every front at least ~1772 x 1299 px so it prints >=300 DPI in the photo window; every back clearly legible for its medium with the postmark preserved; the collection stamp a clean crisp vector; and exactly one finished book page per roster row.

</details>

<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

The Marden Vale Heritage Trust is mounting a wall exhibition, 'Working Lives of the Vale', and needs its five key photographs turned into a cohesive, gallery-quality plate set. We are NOT asking you to invent detail that isn't there — no repainting torn corners, no cloning out scratches, no faking anything our conservator is content to leave as scanned. What ruins a heritage wall is INCONSISTENCY: our five scans came off different originals in different conditions and, side by side, they currently look like five unrelated jobs. Your task is to make them read as ONE exhibition.

We digitized each print on a flatbed, and every frame includes a small neutral grey step-wedge laid on the glass beside the photograph — an honest in-frame reference we place there as standard archival practice. The five photographs are: 'The Reeve Family' (a studio portrait, 1968); 'Quarry Crew, Vale Stone Works' (1946); 'A Draper of the High Street' (a cabinet portrait, 1902); 'Market Row' (a street scene, 1931 — this is our FEATURED image, a single standing trader with a hand on his hip); and 'Canal Wharf' (1955). They reach you in varying conditions — some faded, some colour-shifted, some flat, some sitting off-square on the scanner — and it is your judgement, print by print, to diagnose what each one needs.

The house look we want for the whole set: a warm archival monochrome — a single toned duotone, deep but not blocked-up in the shadows, and above all CONSISTENT from plate to plate so the wall reads as one collection at one common black point. The bar is this: a viewer moving along the wall must not be able to tell the five began life in different conditions — no plate may sit warmer, cooler, lighter or heavier than the rest, and none may carry a leftover colour tinge into the toned result. Correct each scan on its own terms so they all converge on that one shared target. When you're done, hand us a short sheet listing, per scan, the white-balance, exposure and black-point moves you dialled and the single archival tone you settled the whole set on, so we can confirm the collection was matched to one target rather than eyeballed frame by frame.

Then three finishing pieces. FEATURED CUTOUT: from the market-row scene, lift the standing trader cleanly off his background onto our archival-cream card for the exhibition entrance panel. He stands with a hand on his hip, so there is open space under his bent arm and between his cap and his shoulder; those see-through gaps must read as clean cream, exactly like the ground around him, and must not fill in solid. EMBLEM: our Trust emblem exists only as a flat scan on off-white paper — clean it up and turn it into crisp vector art for the exhibition signage, labels and the plate headers, so it holds razor-sharp at any size. PLATES: we have hand-built the InDesign exhibition-plate template with the real placeholder fields, an image slot and an emblem slot, and we're giving you the caption sheet — bind them so every photograph gets its own A4 plate with its toned image placed, our emblem in the header, and its plate number, title, date, catalogue reference and caption set in type. Hand back one press-ready 300 DPI A4 PDF covering all five plates, one page per photograph. Set the captions verbatim from our sheet — do not rewrite our catalogue copy.

Deliverables: the five matched archival-duotone masters, the featured trader cutout on cream, the vector emblem, and the press-ready A4 exhibition-plate PDF (one captioned plate per scan).

</details>

Gable & Grove Home Services is a new premium-but-warm home-services company (tagline: 'Clean. Caring. Consistent.') and we're rolling our brand out everywhere at once — trucks, crew shirts, yard signs, the office. Our mark and our one-page usage-guide layout are already designed and signed off; what we need from you is the production, and it has to look like one brand, not eight. Here is what we're sending. First, eight photographs of the mark actually applied in the field: a van door panel, a crew polo, a yard sign staked on a lawn, a folding sidewalk A-frame, a hard-hat decal, our storefront window vinyl, a canvas equipment tote, and a printed job invoice on a clipboard — one photo each, shot by different crew members at different job sites on different days under whatever light was there (some cool and overcast, some under warm shop lights, one under greenish garage fluorescents, a couple over- or under-exposed). Straight out of the folder they look like a jumble, and a usage guide where the same brand looks a different colour on every page reads amateur. To keep it honest we laid a photographic 18% grey card into the corner of every shot. Your job on the photos: bring every one to a consistent, true-to-material look by neutralizing each to the grey card it carries — the card must read as a clean neutral grey in your finished frame, and once every card is neutral the whole rollout sits on one white point. Do NOT force one blanket correction across the batch — each shot was lit differently and needs its own white-balance and exposure decision to land on the shared target; some frames need warming, others need cooling, and pushing the same numbers through all of them will leave the set mismatched. Be careful and look at what's actually in each frame before you move it — at least one of these surfaces is a genuinely warm, earthy material and its colour is correct as shot; do not 'cool a cast' that isn't there or you'll drain the material we're selling. Second, our brand terracotta has to match: the exact same ink photographs slightly different on painted van vinyl, on embroidered thread and on printed corrugated board, and on the guide those have to read as ONE house terracotta — bring them together without touching the rest of each photo and without flipping the colour to some other hue; it's a deepen-and-settle within the same warm red-orange family, not a jump to a new colour. Third, isolate each branded item cleanly onto an even ground for the guide, and — this is where our last vendor failed — keep the see-through gaps see-through: the open space between the tote's carry handles, the open V under the A-frame's legs, the gaps around the yard-sign's stake legs must NOT get bricked in with solid colour. Fourth, the 'logo files': we've dropped three files in a folder called logo-files and honestly they look interchangeable, but they are not — figure out which ones can become clean scalable vector art for large-format signage and which one cannot survive that and should stay a high-resolution image. Turn the ones that can into a crisp vector master (and a vector icon), and keep the other one as a clean transparent image. Finally, build the guide: we've hand-built the InDesign usage-guide template with the real placeholder fields and two image slots (one for the placement photo, one for our mark), and we're giving you the placement sheet; merge them so every placement gets its own page — the surface name, the reproduction method, the minimum size and the clear-space note bound in, the cleaned placement photo dropped into the photo window and our vector mark dropped into the mark window — then hand back one press-ready ~300 DPI PDF, one page per placement. Bind the copy verbatim from the sheet; don't rewrite our reproduction specs. Acceptance: every grey card neutral and the whole set on one white point (tell us, per photo, the final white-balance and exposure move you landed on so we can trust it's matched and not eyeballed); the brand terracotta matched to one house value across the surfaces; the open gaps still see-through; the mark files prepped the correct way each; and exactly one finished usage-guide page per placement row.

</details>

Do NOT force one blanket correction across all eight: each frame was lit differently and needs its own white-balance and exposure judgement to land on that shared neutral, and every garment's genuine product colour must be preserved — no garment pushed off the colour we are actually selling. When you are done, tell us the final white-balance and exposure move you made on each frame, and the final pixel size of each, so we can confirm the set is matched and that each photo is still sharp in the hangtag photo window (that window is 70 x 90 mm and at press resolution it needs at least ~827 x 1063 px of real image — a garment cropped down to a small web thumbnail will print soft, which we will reject). Second, the brand marks for print: you have our flat two-colour lockup (a stencil-cut OVERDRIVE wordmark plus a graduation-cap glyph, navy and varsity-gold) and a close-up photo of our printed metallic-foil chenille patch (the premium 'Founders' tier mark, all sheen and rainbow catch-light). Third — this is the part a print shop cannot do without you — give us BURNABLE SEPARATIONS from the lockup: film positives ready to burn screens, one screen per ink colour, each colour's artwork as a solid black positive on a clear film base with the letter counters open. Finally, build the tags: we have hand-built the InDesign hangtag template with the real placeholder fields and two image slots (the product photo and the tier mark), and we are giving you the 12-SKU roster; merge them so every SKU gets its own hangtag with its name, code, colourway, size, fabric, price and size-graded print placement bound in, its neutralized product photo dropped into the photo window, and its correct tier mark in the mark window — then hand back a press-ready ~300 DPI PDF, one hangtag per SKU. <details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

Steelyard Haul-Off is a junk-removal, cleanout and light-demolition company rolling out new fleet and crew branding across box trucks, roll-off containers, crew tees, car magnets, yard signs and a storefront window. Their palette is black, safety lime-green and steel grey, and the mark is a bold stencil-block 'SY' monogram sitting above the 'STEELYARD' wordmark and a thin tagline. They need a professional, print-and-wrap-ready brand rollout package.

What you are given: TWO reference images of the mark (they only ever had it as raster, no vector source on file), six recent photographs of their fleet, crew and yard taken for the brand book, a placement roster listing every surface the brand will land on with its substrate, size, minimum clear space and required colorway, and a hand-built page-layout template for the spec sheets.

The job:
1) Produce the clean, scalable vector MASTER of the full lockup, print-ready with crisp edges and the black / lime / steel-grey palette intact - work from whichever of the two supplied references actually rebuilds into clean vector geometry, and get the other one delivered in the form it is actually good for.
2) From the master, build the rest of the mark FAMILY: a two-tone monogram-only icon for app tiles and embroidery; a single-color version for one-color screen-print, vinyl cutting and stamps; a reversed treatment that reads correctly on dark substrates; and a high-impact lime-on-black hero to splash large across a trailer side. Each of these is a different production need - use the treatment that genuinely produces each one, not one blanket effect relabelled five times.
3) Make the six brand photographs read as ONE set. They were shot on different days under different light, so out of the folder they do not match. Each frame carries an 18% grey card in shot as a reference; neutralize every frame to it so the whole set lands on one common, true house white point with a subtle honest daylight warmth - deep shadows that stay open, highlights on chrome and hi-vis that do not blow. Because each frame started under different light, matching the OUTPUT means each frame needs its OWN correction reasoned from its OWN card - a single blanket setting across the batch will not match, and one of the shots is of a genuinely lime-green subject under clean light, so do not chase a cast that is not there. When done, hand back the white-balance and exposure moves you settled on per frame so we can confirm the set was matched, not eyeballed, and crop the grey card out of the finals.
4) Assemble the deliverable: we have hand-built the page-layout template with the real placeholder fields and two image slots (one for the placement's logo colorway, one for its brand photo). Merge it against the roster so every placement gets its own single-page spec sheet - the surface name, substrate, size, clear-space rule and palette callouts (hex / CMYK / spot-ink) bound as copy, with the correct colorway artwork and the matching graded photo dropped in - and hand back one press-ready ~300 DPI US Letter PDF covering every placement, one page per placement, the flagship placement first.

Hard rules: original vector geometry rebuilt from our supplied artwork, no from-scratch redraw, no generative fill or object removal, no compositing, no upscaling; the color sheet and type are actually set through the merge, not handed off.

</details>

<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

Evergreen, a dispensary chain, is putting its Fall/Spring elevated-streetwear apparel capsule into production and needs the front and back prints handed to our screen-print shop as art the exposure room can actually burn. We are NOT redesigning anything -- the designer has already hand-painted the capsule's crest panels and we are preparing what we were given for the press.

We are sending you the panels as flatbed scans. Fair warning up front: they were painted and scanned across two different sessions on different days, so they do NOT match -- some are cooler and a little dim, others warmer and brighter, and each sits a little crooked on the bed. Every painted panel has a small 18% grey reference swatch and corner registration ticks in its bottom margin. Before you touch anything else, get each panel's paper reading as one clean, identical, neutral white by eye off that grey swatch, using whatever straighten angle and temperature/tint/exposure moves THAT panel needs -- if the panels are cleaned to different whites, the brand purples drift and the six garments won't read as one drop. Tell us, per panel, the straighten angle and the tone/white-balance moves you settled on, so we can trust they really are matched.

Our shop rules, and the bar each panel must hit -- part of the job is deciding, per panel, which situation you are looking at, because getting it wrong won't show until it's on a shirt: (1) our manual press holds a limited number of screens and every ink prints as its own solid screen, so a design built from flat spot colours must come back as clean crisp VECTOR separation art where each colour is a solid holdable shape, one solid screen per ink. (2) A background has to be GENUINELY transparent -- if a panel still carries a stray off-white paper matte or halo, that matte burns as a phantom screen and prints as a ghost box, so it must be truly knocked out before anything else, not just look clean on screen. (3) The brand palette is locked (deep purple #4B2E83, black #0B0B0B, and pink #E8669E in intentional places only); if a panel carries a stray hand-mixed accent that is off that palette, or secretly uses several near-identical tones of what is really ONE ink, those have to be brought back onto one holdable screen before tracing -- we are not burning extra screens to print what should be one. (4) Some art is not spot-separable at all: anything built from smooth painted washes, blends or soft bleeds is continuous tone, and a manual mesh cannot hold unlimited tones -- that art has to be reseparated into a single HALFTONE screen (one ink, dot pattern) the mesh can hold, and it is exactly the panel where we want the worn, premium distress texture the house's elevated-streetwear direction is known for, so give it a subtle grain pass. Do NOT leave a wash as a gradient and do NOT force-trace it into a tangle of vector paths that will never register.

One more thing: not everything in the folder is artwork. One file is a photo of a finished printed tee on fabric -- it's only there so you can see how the ink sits. It must NOT go anywhere near the tracer; give us a clean webshop cut-out of it instead. Also vectorise the plain wordmark bitmap into scalable line art for the decorator.

Deliverables: each panel's finished separation in the correct form; the wordmark line art; the tee packshot; and a laid-up SEPARATION SELL-SHEET -- one page per panel -- that drops each finished separation into our template alongside its garment placement, print size and ink-limit note from the production roster we're sending, exported press-ready so the exposure room and the client both have one clean reference. Bind the roster copy verbatim -- don't rewrite our placements or sizes. Keep everything spot / halftone oriented for screen print -- no process-colour conversion, no new artwork, no recolouring a design to a different palette.

</details>

Larkfield Party Co. prints a per-event promotional product catalog and matching shelf price tags, one card and one tag per SKU, driven from a spreadsheet (one row per SKU: product name, blurb, price, SKU code, event name). Our recurring headache is that long product names and blurbs overflow the frame and get clipped on export — the layout won't shrink them to fit on its own. We have already rebuilt both templates ourselves in a professional page-layout program with 'auto-size / shrink text to fit frame' switched on for every variable-data frame and real merge fields wired up (ProductName, Blurb, Price, SKU, EventName), so the layouts are now overset-safe; we are handing them to you as finished template files and we do not want them redesigned. What we need from you is everything that flows INTO those templates. First, the photography: we are sending eight existing product shots and NOT reshooting. They were taken over a couple of afternoons under whatever light was around — some cool, some warm, a couple too dark or too bright — so out of the folder they look like a mismatched jumble, and a catalog of mismatched shots reads cheap. To make matched-ness checkable we laid a photographic 18% grey card into the corner of every shot. Bring the whole set to one consistent, true-to-product look by neutralizing each image to the grey card it contains until that card reads as a clean neutral grey; once every card is neutral the set will share one white point. Hold a subtle warm, celebratory feel in the final look, but do NOT force one blanket correction across the batch — each shot was lit differently and needs its own white-balance, exposure and tone decision to land on the shared target, and neutralize to the CARD, not to an assumed cast: some of these products are genuinely warm-colored, and if a product's own color is already warm you must not cool it chasing a cast that isn't there, or you strip the very color we are selling. When you are done, tell us the final white-balance and exposure move you settled on for each frame so we can confirm the set is matched, not eyeballed. Second, a seasonal colorway without a reshoot: on the hero SKU (the foil number-balloon bundle) the ribbon is currently a bright red — give us a deeper gala-burgundy version of that same shot, a rich dark wine-red in the same color family, and the recolor has to sit under the ribbon's real folds, sheen and shadow with the rest of the product untouched — no flat dead color, no whole-image tint bleeding onto the balloons. Third, our wordmark only exists as a flat scan on off-white paper and looks fuzzy at print size — get it clean and razor-sharp as vector art so it stays crisp wherever it lands in the layouts. Finally, build the pieces: merge the roster into BOTH of our auto-fit templates — the catalog (one A4 card per SKU, carrying that SKU's graded photo and the wordmark) and the shelf tags (one small tag per SKU, carrying the wordmark) — so every row becomes its own page, long records shrink to fit via the templates' auto-size instead of clipping, and hand back two press-ready PDFs: the catalog at A4 with 3mm bleed and the tags at tag size, both ~300 DPI. Bind our copy and prices verbatim from the roster; do not rewrite them. The whole point: long records must render legibly through the templates' auto-fit, never clipped, and the photos must read as one matched set.

</details>

<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

Maple Cricket League (MCL) is a streetwear-forward street/backyard cricket league for the diaspora community. The identity is already designed; we need the production-art thread executed and handed back as clean, organised, correctly named files. Our own team handles the website, the written brand voice and the social templates — do NOT build those here.

What we are sending you:
• Six brand photos of our street-cricket sessions. Fair warning: they were shot on different days in very different light and they do NOT match out of camera — some warm, some cold, some flat, some contrasty. On the edge of every frame the shooter left a neutral 18% grey card and a small white chip so the set can be brought to a common white balance after the fact. One of them also came in a few degrees off level.
• A flat scan of the logo-system art sheet (crest + monogram + hat badge laid out together, two flat ink colours on paper).
• Our authored multi-artboard vector master of those same three marks, already built and ready to hand to the factory.
• A photo of the away-kit chest crest — one dark ink on near-white fabric — that came in slightly rotated and off-centre.
• A studio flat of a folded home jersey on a seamless sweep, and a close photo of the embroidered crest patch on a cap.

The bar (this is the whole job):
1. BRAND PHOTOGRAPHY — the six frames have to read as ONE brand. Every frame must resolve to the SAME house look: the neutral grey card in each lands truly neutral (no residual warm or cool cast) at one common white point, the shadows sit on one common deep-but-not-crushed near-black floor that never clips a channel to zero, the palette pulled toward a muted, filmic street tone with skin kept alive and speculars held. Because the frames start from different casts and exposures, each one needs a DIFFERENT correction to hit that shared target — a set that is each 'auto-fixed' to look fine on its own will not agree at the grey cards and we will reject it. Author the look on the strongest frame first, then match the rest to it. Level the crooked frame. Hand back a short sheet listing, per frame, the white balance / exposure / black-point you dialed, so we can confirm the set was matched to one target and not eyeballed frame by frame. Then give us the strongest frame reframed into a wide site/social HEADER, using the room already in the shot, with clean empty space on one side for a headline — no invented canvas.
2. LOGO SYSTEM — turn the flat art sheet into clean, infinitely-scalable vector artwork, and separately export our authored vector master to a print-ready vector file (plus a raster preview) for the factory. Do not redraw or reinvent the marks.
3. AWAY CREST PRINT — turn the away-kit crest into a one-colour, print-ready screen/sublimation separation at print resolution: get it square and level, cropped tight to the print bounds, and rendered as a single-ink treatment the factory can burn.
4. MERCH CUT-OUTS — give us clean transparent cut-outs of the folded jersey and of the cap for the lookbook / e-commerce.

Hard rules: no inventing new artwork, no from-scratch logo or lettering, no generative fill or canvas extension, no compositing one image onto another. The vector master export must come from the authored master file we supply. Every step after each asset loads must build on a previous result.

</details>

Kanaka Mahal is a traditional catering & events hall and we are running our Maalai Vizha festive-season promotion across seven branches — one large-format vinyl banner per branch, each printed at 12 ft x 6 ft and read from across a busy street, so it has to look rich, warm and unmistakably from one brand. First, the premises photos: seven shots, one of each branch's decorated frontage/stage, but here is the problem — they were taken by different branch managers on different evenings under whatever festival lighting was up (some under warm tungsten string-lights, some under cool white LED wash, one under greenish work-lights and dim, one badly over-exposed against the evening sky, one strong blue open-shade), so straight out of the folder they look like seven unrelated pictures. A banner series where every branch has a different colour cast looks cheap and off-brand. To make this checkable we laid a photographic 18% grey card into a corner of every shot. Your job on the photos: bring every image to one consistent, true-to-life festive look by neutralizing each one to the grey card it contains — the card must read as a clean neutral grey in your finished frame, and once every card is neutral the whole series shares one white point and one warmth. Do NOT force one blanket correction across all seven: each was lit differently and needs its own white-balance and exposure decision to land on the shared target — some frames need warming, some need cooling, one is a colour problem on a second axis, one needs its blown highlights pulled back first. Be careful: at least one branch's frontage is genuinely, deeply gold — real brass lamps and marigold under warm-but-neutral light — and if its grey card already reads neutral you must NOT 'cool a blue cast' that isn't there or you will strip the exact festive colour we are selling. When you are done, tell us the final white-balance and exposure move you made on each frame AND the final pixel size of each hero crop, so we can confirm the set is matched and that every banner will hold up at print size: each hero drops into a large hero window on the 12 x 6 ft banner and at our large-format print resolution that window needs at least ~4320 x 2160 px of real image — a photo cropped down small will print soft and pixelated across a 12-foot banner, which we will reject, and we do not accept any upscaling to fake it. Second, a colour fix without a reshoot: on the branch whose entrance is draped in a bright pillar-box RED cloth, give us a version where that drape is our deep-maroon house colour instead (a rich, dark maroon/burgundy in the SAME warm-red family, just deepened and muted — not a jump to a far-off hue), and the recolour has to sit under the real folds, sheen and shadow of the cloth, touching ONLY the drape — no flat dead colour, no whole-image tint bleeding onto the lamps and people. Third, a traditional touch: derive a screen-print / halftone texture motif from one of the graded heroes so the banner carries a printed-poster feel up close; it drops into a fixed texture panel in our layout. Fourth, the brand marks: we are giving you two logo files — our flat two-colour crest, and a close-up PHOTOGRAPH of the embossed gold-foil seal from our premises signboard. Prep both so they drop cleanly into the banner and stay sharp at print size — but they are NOT the same kind of file and must not be treated the same way; think about which one can honestly become clean line art and which one would be destroyed by that. Fifth, we still have last year's banner only as a flattened proof PDF — convert it back into an editable InDesign source so we can reuse the frame next year. Finally, build the banners: we have hand-built the InDesign banner template with the real placeholder fields and the image slots (hero, crest, foil seal, and texture panel), and we are giving you the branch roster; merge them so every branch gets its own single banner with its name, address, phone, offer line and valid dates bound in, its graded hero dropped into the hero window, the crisp crest and the foil seal in their windows, and the halftone motif in the texture panel — then hand back a press-ready banner per branch. Bind the branch copy verbatim from the roster — do not rewrite our addresses, offers or dates. Acceptance: every grey card neutral and the whole series on one white point while the genuinely-gold branch keeps its real colour; every hero crop at least ~4320 x 2160 px with no upscaling; the drape recolour natural under the existing light and confined to the cloth; the crest a clean vector and the foil seal a sharp raster that still looks like foil; and exactly one press-ready banner per roster row.

<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

TitanSeal is a Gulf-based B2B private-label industrial-sealants brand launching three SKUs. The master logo is approved and supplied to you as one high-resolution PNG on a solid white ground (the wordmark 'TitanSeal' with a solid caulk-bead droplet icon, in deep industrial blue). Using ONLY the Adobe connector, deliver four things.

The supplied file sits on a solid white ground, so think about the order of operations — a mark still carrying its white field will trace or recolor as a white-bounded block. Note also that our droplet icon is a solid open shape but the wordmark letters have enclosed counters; if a clean one-color reversed wordmark for a dark ground is not achievable with these tools, deliver the reversed treatment from the icon instead and tell us why, rather than shipping a wordmark with filled-in letter holes.

SECOND, the DIGITAL PACK. We are NOT reshooting. The jobsite folder was shot across a single day under whatever light was there — cold overcast outside, warm tungsten in a fit-out corner, greenish strip-lighting in a bay, golden late sun — and a couple of frames are tilted and one is dark, so straight out of the folder they look like a mismatched jumble and a launch feed of mismatched shots reads cheap. To make consistency checkable we laid an 18% grey card into a corner of every frame. Bring the whole set to one consistent, true-to-material look by neutralizing each frame to the grey card it contains (the card must read as clean neutral grey, equal across the channels, in your finished frame) so that once every card is neutral the set shares one white point; hold a subtle cool-industrial house feel in the final look, but do NOT force one blanket correction across the folder — each frame was lit differently and needs its own white-balance, exposure, and tone decision to land on the shared target. Be careful with the frame whose hero subject is a bead of our GREY sealant: grey product under neutral light is not a colour cast — if that frame's card already reads neutral, do not 'warm' or 'cool' it chasing an imagined cast, or you will throw off the very material we are selling. When you are done, tell us the final white-balance and exposure move you made on each frame so we can confirm the set is matched, not eyeballed. From the matched set, size the platform tiles we need: a 1:1 social tile, a 16:9 web banner, a slim email-signature strip, and a 1:1 messaging-catalog card — each framed on the work, with the grey card cropped OUT of the delivered tile.

THIRD, the LABELS. We have hand-built the InDesign wrap-label template with the real placeholder fields and a logo image frame, and we are giving you the roster; merge them so every SKU gets its own single-page label with its name, code, volume, colorway and barcode bound from the roster and the brand mark dropped into its frame, then hand back one press-ready label PDF covering every SKU (one page per SKU). Bind the copy verbatim from the roster — do not rewrite our codes or volumes.

FOURTH, the CARTONS. We have hand-built the Illustrator carton die-line with named Variables and the mono mark already placed in the art; repopulate the text variables from the roster for the 20-cartridge and 24-tube packs and export the single-color carton artwork to PDF with the die-line preserved.

Acceptance: every grey card neutral (channel spread within a hair of zero) and the whole jobsite set matched to one white point while the grey-sealant frame keeps its true material colour; the logo system derived from the one supplied mark with the correct prep/trace order and an honest reversed treatment; exactly one finished label per roster row; and the single-color carton PDF with its die-line intact. OUT OF SCOPE for the connector (flag as human/desktop finishing): authoring the brand-standards PDF body and typography pages, drawing any new layout from scratch, and the marketplace listing-page composition.
