<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

Cindergrove is a small online coffee-goods shop refreshing its storefront, and I need one cohesive set of graphics that instantly reads as a sleek, modern space. Three areas of scope. (1) PRODUCT CARDS — the heart of it: a clean product-detail card for every item, each carrying the product name, SKU, price and a short blurb next to a high-quality photo, with our shop mark crisp at the top. We are NOT reshooting. I'm handing you eight product photos we already have, and here's the problem: they were shot over a few sessions in whatever corner had space, so straight out of the folder they're a mismatched jumble — some under cool shop fluorescents, some under warm window light, a couple under an amber lamp, one shot dark, one blown out. A storefront of mismatched product shots looks cheap. So we clipped a small 18% grey card into the corner of every shot. Your job on the photos: bring every image to a consistent, true-to-product look by neutralizing each one to the grey card it carries — the card must read as a clean neutral grey in your finished frame, and once every card is neutral the whole set shares one white point. Hold a subtle warm, premium feel across all of them, but do NOT force one blanket correction on the batch: each photo was lit differently and needs its own white-balance, exposure and tone decision to land on the shared target. Be careful — at least one product is genuinely warm-toned (some of our stoneware is a real terracotta color); if that shot's grey card already reads neutral, do not 'cool' it chasing a cast that isn't there, or you'll strip the color we're selling. When you're done, tell me the final white-balance and exposure move you made on each frame so I can confirm they're matched, not eyeballed. Carry ONE deliberate house look across the whole set — a restrained warm-highlight, cool-neutral-shadow tone with modest contrast and a gentle, not-garish color lift — so every card feels art-directed by the same hand; the catch our last freelancer missed is letting the color lift go loud and cartoonish, so keep it balanced. (2) A SEASONAL COLORWAY without a reshoot: one of our shots is the bright-red enamel kettle — give me a deeper seasonal burgundy version of the SAME shot (a rich, dark wine-red in the same family, just deepened and slightly muted, not a jump to a far-off hue), and the recolor has to sit under the real folds, highlights and shadows of the enamel so it still looks like a photograph of that kettle — no flat dead color, no whole-image tint bleeding onto the counter and the other props, just the kettle body. (3) STOREFRONT DRESSING — the hero banner sized for BOTH desktop (1920x720) and mobile (1080x1350), built from the one product hero shot that has generous empty space around it so you can reframe it to both shapes by cropping (no invented pixels); plus our icon/divider set and one accent graphic for the section breaks. Two notes on the marks: our shop wordmark only exists as a flat scan on off-white paper — get it clean and razor-sharp as a vector for the card header (it must not look like a fuzzy scan when printed), and separately we have a photo of our painted storefront decal on a textured wall that we want lifted onto a clean transparent ground as a section accent — that one is a photograph, so treat it as a photograph. Finally, build the cards: we've hand-built the InDesign product-card template with the real placeholder fields and two image slots (one for the product photo, one for the shop mark at the top), and here's the roster; merge them so every SKU gets its own single card with its copy bound, its matching graded photo dropped in, and the crisp shop mark in the header, then hand back one press-ready PDF covering every SKU — one page per SKU. Bind the copy verbatim from the roster; do not rewrite our names or prices. Acceptance: every grey card neutral and the whole set on one white point with the house warmth held; the kettle recolor natural under the existing light; the shop mark a clean vector; the banner at both sizes from real cropped pixels; and exactly one finished card per roster row.

<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

Cinder & Reed Festival 2027 is a two-stage boutique showcase, and we need the physical performer laminate passes produced from our confirmed lineup — one personalised pass per performer, worn on a lanyard, that has to look sharp and consistent on stage and on camera. Our brand and the pass layout are already signed off; what we need is the production. We are handing you everything the job needs. First, the headshots: eight performer photos, but here is the problem — they were shot by different stage photographers across load-in and soundcheck under whatever light was around (some under cool LED wash, some under warm tungsten, one under greenish work-lights, a couple over- or under-exposed), so straight out of the folder they look like eight different shoots. A row of passes where every face has a different colour cast looks amateur. To make this checkable we laid a photographic 18% grey card into the corner of every shot. Your job on the photos: bring every headshot to one consistent, true-to-skin look by neutralizing each one to the grey card it contains — the card must read as a clean neutral grey in your finished frame, and once every card is neutral the whole set shares one white point and one exposure feel. Do NOT force one blanket correction across all eight: each was lit differently and needs its own white-balance and exposure decision to land on the shared target — some frames need warming, others need cooling, and pushing the same numbers through all of them will leave the set mismatched. When you are done, tell us the final white-balance and exposure move you made on each frame, and the final pixel size of each headshot, so we can confirm the set is matched and that every face will still be sharp at print size. That last part matters: each pass drops the headshot into a 60 x 75 mm photo window, and at press resolution that window needs at least ~709 x 886 px of real image — a face cropped down to a small web thumbnail will print soft and blurry, which we will reject. Second, the access-tier marks: three of them sit on the passes depending on the performer's tier — two are flat two-colour crests (ARTIST and SUPPORT), and the third, the AAA all-access mark, is a photograph of our printed holographic foil sample with all its sheen and rainbow gradient. All three need to be prepped so they drop cleanly into the pass's mark window and stay sharp at print size — but they are not the same kind of file and should not be treated the same way; think about which one can become clean line art and which one cannot survive that. Finally, build the passes: we have hand-built the InDesign laminate template with the real placeholder fields and two image slots (headshot and tier mark), and we are giving you the lineup roster; merge them so every performer gets their own single pass with their name, stage and access tier bound in, their neutralized headshot dropped into the photo window, and their tier mark in the mark window — then hand back a press-ready ~300 DPI PDF, one pass per performer. Bind the names, stages and tiers verbatim from the roster — do not invent or reassign anyone; some performer names are long and must fit the auto-size name frame without clipping. Acceptance: every grey card neutral and the whole set on one white point; every headshot at least ~709 x 886 px so it prints >=300 DPI in the 60 x 75 mm window; the three tier marks each prepped the correct way and razor-sharp at print size; and exactly one finished laminate per roster row.

</details>

Your job on the photos: bring every headshot to one consistent, true-to-skin look by neutralizing each one to the grey card it contains — the card must read as a clean neutral grey (equal across the channels) in your finished frame, and once every card is neutral the whole set shares one white point and one exposure feel. Do NOT force one blanket correction across all nine: each was lit differently and needs its own white-balance and exposure decision to land on the shared target — some frames need warming, others cooling, one needs the green pulled out on the tint axis, a couple need real exposure recovery. And be careful with skin: at least one of our agents has a genuinely warm, deep complexion and was shot under clean neutral light, so that frame's grey card already reads neutral — do not 'cool' it chasing a cast that is not there, or you will strip the real skin tone and the card will look wrong. When you are done, tell us the final white-balance and exposure move you made on each frame, and the final pixel size of each headshot, so we can confirm the set is matched and that every face will still be sharp at print size. That last part matters: each card drops the headshot into a 40 x 50 mm photo window, and at press resolution that window needs at least ~472 x 591 px of real image — a face cropped down to a small thumbnail will print soft and blurry, which we will reject. Second, the tier seals: three of them sit on the cards depending on the agent's production tier — Standard, Preferred and President's Council. They all need to drop cleanly into the card's seal window and stay razor-sharp at print size and keep their finish — but they did not all come to you as the same kind of file, and treating them all the same way will quietly wreck one of them. Look at each before you decide how to prep it. Third, our wordmark: it only exists as a flat printed mark on a piece of cream letterhead, slightly skewed on the scan with paper margin around it — get it clean, straight and razor-sharp for the card, not a fuzzy paper-bounded scan. Finally, build the cards: we have hand-built the InDesign counter-card template with the real placeholder fields and three image slots (headshot, tier seal and wordmark), and we are giving you the producer roster; merge them so every agent gets their own single card with their details bound in verbatim, their neutralized headshot in the photo window, their correct tier seal in the seal window and the wordmark in the masthead — then hand back a press-ready ~300 DPI A6 PDF, one card per producer. <details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

Thistledown Press is a small independent children's-book imprint about to upload its next paperback, 'The Lantern Fox', to Amazon KDP. The last title we sent up bounced in preflight because the interior pages did not print consistently and the cover art was off, so this time we want a print specialist to actually FINISH the files, not just check them. The manuscript, the caption text, and all the artwork already exist — we are NOT re-illustrating and we do NOT want anything redrawn. Here is the situation and what a print-ready result has to look like. First, the illustrations. Our illustrator painted the story in gouache and we scanned the ten story-page paintings, but not all in one sitting: half were captured on the flatbed one afternoon (they come out cool and slightly blue) and half were shot on the copy stand another evening under our old warm work lights (they come out warm and orange), and a few of the paintings sat a little crooked when they were captured. On the scan bed beside every painting we laid a photographic neutral grey step-wedge so there is an honest reference to balance against. Straight out of the folder the set is a jumble — the same cream page-paper looks blue in one scan and amber in the next — and a picture book whose pages don't share a page-white looks cheap and gets rejected. Your job on the artwork: bring every scan to a consistent, true look by neutralizing each one to the grey wedge it carries, so the wedge reads as a clean neutral and, once every wedge is neutral, the whole book shares ONE page-white. Each painting was lit differently and needs its OWN white-balance and exposure decision to land there — do not force one blanket correction across the batch. Be careful with the nightfall page ('the fox on the starlit hill'): that illustration is SUPPOSED to glow warm amber from the lantern, and it was captured cleanly so its grey wedge already reads neutral — do NOT cool it chasing an imagined orange cast or you will kill the mood the whole book builds to. When you are done, tell us the final white-balance and exposure move you made on each scan so we can confirm the set is genuinely matched, not eyeballed. Second, continuity: the fox wears a red scarf, and because the three pages it appears on came from different sessions the scarf currently reads cold-maroon on one page, muddy on the dark hollow-tree page, and orange on the warm market page. Bring the scarf to ONE consistent house crimson on all three — a rich true red in the same family, deepened or warmed just enough to match, riding the real folds and shadow of the cloth, not a flat painted patch and not a tint that bleeds onto the fox or the background. Third, our imprint colophon only exists as the mark inked on a piece of off-white paper; get it clean and razor-sharp as scalable art for the cover and title page — it must not look like a fuzzy scan when printed. Finally, build the files. We have hand-built two InDesign shells: an illustrated-interior-page template with a full-bleed picture frame and the caption type fields, and a wraparound-cover template (back, spine, front on one sheet) with the spine already sized for our page count. We are giving you the story-caption sheet (one row per illustrated page, in reading order) and the cover sheet. Merge them: drop each finished illustration into its page with the caption bound from our sheet, and build the wraparound cover with the finished cover painting, the vectorized imprint mark, and the title and back-cover copy in place. Hand back the illustrated interior as ONE press-ready PDF with one page per caption row at KDP's 8.5x11 in trim with 0.125 in bleed and 300 DPI artwork, and the wraparound cover as its own press-ready PDF. Bind our caption and cover copy verbatim — do not rewrite it. Acceptance: every grey wedge neutral and the set matched to one page-white; the scarf one crimson on all three pages; the imprint mark a crisp vector; and exactly one interior page per caption row.

</details>

Emberwell Brew House is a warm neighborhood café refreshing its menu for the counter and the tables. Rather than one crowded sheet, we print the menu as a set of small feature cards — one card per item — that sit in the holders by the register and on the tables, and the same set doubles as our posts and delivery-app photos. We have the card template built and the copy written; what we need is the imagery brought up to standard and the cards produced.

Here is the problem with the photos. Our staff shot the food and drinks over one busy morning in whatever spot was free — some by the cool front window, some under the warm pendant lamps over the bar, a couple in the dim back corner, one or two out on the sunny patio — so straight out of the folder they are a mismatched jumble: some cool and blue, some warm and amber, one or two underexposed, one blown out and hot, and several sitting at a slight tilt. A set of cards that don't match reads cheap. Because we knew the light was a mess, whoever shot them clipped a small neutral grey card into the corner of every frame. Your job on the imagery: bring the whole batch to ONE deliberately warm, cozy, appetizing look by neutralizing each capture against the grey card it carries — the card must read as a clean neutral grey in your finished frame, and once every card is neutral the whole set shares one white point. Then carry a single house look across all of them: a warm, morning-light feel — gently warm highlights, clean neutral shadows, a little contrast and clarity, a restrained vibrance lift — so every card feels like it came from the same shoot. Do NOT force one blanket correction across the batch: each capture was lit differently and needs its own white-balance, exposure, and tone decision to land on the shared look. And be careful with the dishes that are supposed to be a strong color — the butter croissant is genuinely deep golden and one of the drinks is a true bright red; if a dish's grey card already reads neutral, do not 'correct' a cast that isn't there, and do not let the warm grade drag our green plates (the avocado toast, the matcha) toward a dull olive. When you're done, tell us the white-balance and exposure move you made on each frame so we can confirm they were matched, not eyeballed. Second, a seasonal card without a reshoot: our signature iced cooler is a bright hibiscus red today — give us a deeper, spiced-cranberry / mulled version of that same shot for the seasonal card (a rich, dark berry-red in the SAME family, just deepened and slightly muted, not a jump to a new hue), and the new color has to sit under the real highlights, ice and shadow of the drink, not as a flat dead fill or a wash over the whole glass and table. Third, our wordmark only exists as a flat piece on warm off-white paper, slightly crooked — get it clean and razor-sharp as a vector so it sits crisp at the top of every card and scales to the A-frame board. Fourth, back the cards with a warm kraft / linen texture — source one you like. Finally, build the cards: we have hand-built the InDesign card template with the real placeholder fields and the image slots, and we're giving you the roster; merge them so every menu item gets its own single-page card with its copy bound, its matching graded photo dropped in, the crisp wordmark at the masthead and the kraft behind it, then hand back one press-ready ~300 DPI card per item plus a high-resolution JPEG set for social and the delivery apps. Bind the copy verbatim from the roster — do not rewrite our descriptions or prices. Acceptance: every grey card neutral and the whole batch matched to one warm white point with each dish's true color intact; the cooler recolor natural under its own light; the wordmark a clean skew-free vector; and exactly one finished card per roster row.

<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

Lumen Quarterly is a small independent arts-and-culture magazine. We are closing the Autumn 2026 issue and our feature photography is a mess of mismatched light: the stories were shot by different contributors on different days - some under warm tungsten in studios and workshops, some by cold north-facing windows, one flat and underexposed in a dim archive, one blown-out on a rooftop at noon - so straight out of the folder the issue does not read as ONE magazine, and our board rejects issues that look stitched together. Our brand's imagery rule is that all photography is warm, editorial and consistently graded, with no cold or blue casts and no oversaturation. To give you something honest to balance against, every photographer left a photographic 18% grey card at the edge of frame. Here is the job.

First, the set has to become one room. Bring every one of the ten feature photos to a consistent look by neutralising each frame to the grey card it carries - the card must read as a clean neutral grey in your finished frame - and then settle the whole set onto a single warm-editorial house look: a shared white point, a gentle warm editorial tone in the highlights and shadows, restrained (never punchy) saturation. Do NOT force one blanket correction across the batch: a warm tungsten frame and a cold window frame need opposite white-balance moves to arrive at the same place, and an underexposed archive frame and an overexposed rooftop frame need opposite exposure moves. Be careful with the sound-artist forest frame - it was shot under flat neutral overcast, so its grey card already reads neutral and the woodland genuinely is cool and misty; the warm editorial feeling on that frame must come from the shared TONE you apply to the whole set, not from shoving its white balance warm - if you 'warm out an imagined blue cast' there you will push its neutral card off-neutral and turn a true grey day orange. The warmth is a house tone laid on every frame equally; the white-balance correction is per-frame and driven by each card. When you are done, tell us the white-balance and exposure move you dialed on each frame so we can confirm the set was matched, not eyeballed.

Second, one photo breaks the palette. The ceramics feature ('The Slow Kiln') hero has a stack of glazed bowls in a hot, almost fluorescent tomato-red that reads garish against our warm-editorial palette and trips the 'no oversaturation' rule. Bring just those bowls down into the editorial range - a deeper, softer terracotta in the same red-earth family, muted and darkened, NOT a jump to some far-off hue - and it has to sit under the real glaze: the sheen, the throwing rings and the shadow inside each bowl must survive. Only the bowls - do not desaturate the potter, the kiln or the rest of the frame, and no flat painted-on colour.

Third, our masthead lock-up only exists as a flat scan on off-white paper and it prints fuzzy. Get it clean and razor-sharp as vector art for the opener furniture.

Finally, build the issue. We have hand-built the InDesign feature-opener template with the real placeholder fields - headline, standfirst, pull-quote (which sets in our house coral accent), byline and folio - plus an image frame for the story's hero photo and a masthead frame, and we are giving you the story roster. Merge them so every story gets its own single-page opener with its copy bound and its matching graded hero placed, then hand back a press-ready ~300 DPI A4 PDF of the openers, with the lead feature ('The Slow Kiln') running as the opening page so the editor sees it first. Bind the copy verbatim from the roster - do not rewrite our headlines or standfirsts. Acceptance: every grey card neutral and the whole set matched to one warm-editorial white point and tone; the ceramics bowls softened within their own colour family with the glaze intact; the masthead a clean crisp vector; and exactly one finished opener page per roster row.

</details>

Bind our copy verbatim from the roster — do not rewrite our specs or prices. To make this checkable we laid a photographic 18% grey card into a corner of every frame. Bring the whole set to one consistent, true-to-product look by neutralizing each shot to the grey card it contains — the card must read as a clean neutral grey (equal across the channels) in your finished frame, and once every card is neutral the batch shares one white point. When you are done, tell us the final white-balance and exposure move you made on each frame so we can confirm the set is matched, not eyeballed. Second, a variant colorway without a reshoot: our top SKU photographs with a bright safety-orange nozzle cap, and marketing wants a premium 'Pro' colorway of that same shot where the cap reads as a dark graphite/gunmetal finish instead — a deep, desaturated metallic grey, riding the real highlights and shadow of the cap so the plastic still looks like plastic. Only the cap: no flat dead-fill, no whole-image tint bleeding onto the cartridge body or the background. Third, the marks. Our brand wordmark only exists as a flat scan on off-white paper — get it clean and razor-sharp for the label masthead (it must not look like a fuzzy scan on press). And the regulated GHS hazard pictograms we hand you as small flat rasters must be crisp vectors so they stay sharp at any label size. Finally, build the labels: we have hand-built the InDesign master with the real placeholder fields and four image slots (product photo, hazard pictogram, EAN barcode, and the wordmark masthead), and we are giving you the roster; merge them so every SKU/variant gets its own single label with its German copy and H/P statements bound verbatim, its matching graded photo dropped in, the correct hazard pictogram and barcode placed, and the crisp wordmark in the masthead, then hand back a print-ready ~300 DPI CMYK-with-3mm-bleed PDF covering every row (one page per SKU/variant, the Pro colorway simply among them). Bind the German copy and the CLP H/P statements verbatim from the roster — do not paraphrase our compliance text. We are NOT reshooting. Your job on the photos: bring every image to one consistent, true-to-part look by neutralizing each one to the grey card it contains — the card must read as a clean neutral grey in your finished frame, and once every card is neutral the whole set will share one white point. Do NOT force one blanket correction across the batch: each frame was lit differently and needs its own white-balance and exposure decision to land on the shared target — some need warming, others cooling, and pushing one set of numbers through all of them will leave the set mismatched. When you are done, tell us the final white-balance and exposure move you made on each frame and the final pixel size of each, so we can confirm the set is genuinely matched and that every part will still be sharp at print size: each sheet drops the photo into a 5 x 4 inch product window, and at press resolution that window needs at least ~1500 x 1200 px of real image — a part cropped down to a small web thumbnail will print soft and we will reject it. Second, lift each part cleanly off its cluttered bench and set it on a pure solid-white catalog background with the bench and the grey card gone — the way a distributor catalog shows a part; just the part on white, no messy bench, and the black travel-cable coil is the hard one because it was shot on a dark bench and nearly disappears into it, so isolate it by what it IS, not by brightness. Third, a colorway without a reshoot: our emergency push-button fixture is safety-orange, but we are considering a graphite line and want to see it — give us a version of that same shot with the orange housing turned a deep gunmetal graphite (drained of its orange and darkened, staying a believable metal, NOT a flat painted-on grey), and the recolor has to sit under the real moulding, sheen and shadow of the housing, touching only the housing and not the button, the bezel, or the bench. Fourth, our wordmark only exists as a flat scan on off-white paper — get it clean and razor-sharp for the sheet masthead so it does not look like a fuzzy scan when printed. Finally, build the sheets: we have hand-built the InDesign data-sheet template with the real placeholder fields and two image slots (one for the product photo, one for the wordmark at the top), and we are giving you the parts roster; merge them so every SKU gets its own single-page sheet with its part number, description, voltage, amperage, price and section bound in, its matching isolated photo dropped in, and the crisp wordmark in the masthead — then hand back one press-ready ~300 DPI US Letter PDF, one page per SKU. Ridgeline Rovers FC, an amateur mountain-town football (soccer) club, is ordering embroidered crest patches and sleeve badges from a factory and needs its emblem turned into proper production-ready vector artwork first. That texture and cast make it useless for a factory as-is.

The job: (1) clean the reference so it can be traced — deskew it level, auto-tone to fix the flat exposure, neutralize the green fabric cast so the four thread colors read true, then push contrast hard to crush the woven-fabric texture and drive every element toward a clean, flat, high-contrast silhouette; knock the heathered backing to transparent so the trace has no halo. (2) VECTORIZE the cleaned crest into a clean, scalable SVG — this is the master emblem, and it must stay razor-sharp when the factory scales it to the requested medium 3-6 inch patch size. (3) Because embroidery and woven patches need each color as one flat solid thread, reduce the emblem to FLAT SPOT SEPARATIONS: go element by element, select each color region, and lock it to a single solid ink from the club's 4-color palette (no gradients, no anti-aliased blends), then pull a single-color BLACK OUTLINE plate the factory uses for the merrowed-border stitch path, and re-vectorize the flattened art. (4) Deliver a one-color KNOCKOUT (solid emblem silhouette) the factory can use to cut the twill/felt backing. (5) Export the artwork to vector masters (PDF/PNG/SVG) from a genuine authored .ai so the club and factory have the emblem in every format the press needs before the run.

Palette: forest green #2E5A3A, cream #F2E9D0, slate grey #6B7078, black #111111 outline. Deliverables: master crest SVG, flat spot-separated SVG, black-outline plate, one-color knockout, and exported vector masters. Stitch digitizing (.dst/.pes) is handled by the factory from these vector masters — it is not part of this hand-off.

</details>

<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

Wandergrain Supply Co., a small-batch apparel screen-print shop, is putting its new 'Modern Wanderer' traveller-tee line into production. The designer has handed over four finished graphics -- a passport-stamp badge, a latitude/longitude coordinate mark, a minimalist city skyline, and a compass-rose crest -- and we now need them turned into art the exposure room can actually burn screens from. We are NOT redesigning anything and NOT reshooting; we are preparing what we were given for the press.

Our shop rules, and the bar you must hit for each design: (1) Our manual press holds a limited number of screens, and every ink prints as its OWN solid screen -- so a design built from flat spot colors must come back as clean, crisp VECTOR separation art where each color is a solid holdable shape and any editable type stays sharp vector, not a soft raster. (2) A background has to be genuinely transparent -- if a design still carries a stray off-white matte or halo around it, that matte will burn as a phantom screen and print as a ghost box, so it must be truly knocked out to transparency before anything else, not just look transparent on screen. (3) If a design secretly uses several near-identical tones of what is really one ink, those must be collapsed to a SINGLE screen -- we are not burning three screens to print what should be one. (4) Some art is not spot-separable at all: anything built from smooth gradients, blends, or soft shadows is continuous tone, and a manual press cannot hold unlimited tones -- that art has to be reseparated into a single HALFTONE screen (one ink, dot pattern) that the mesh can actually hold, NOT left as a gradient and NOT force-traced into a tangle of vector shapes that will never register. Part of the job is deciding, per design, which of these situations you are looking at -- get the treatment wrong and the screen either won't burn or will print garbage, and you won't see it until it's on a shirt.

Deliverables: for each of the four graphics, the finished separation art in the correct form (vector spot master for the flat designs; a single-ink halftone separation for the continuous-tone one); plus a laid-up SEPARATION SELL-SHEET -- one page per design -- that drops each finished separation into our template alongside its garment placement, print size and ink-limit note from the production roster we're sending, exported press-ready so the exposure room and the client both have a single clean reference. Bind the roster copy verbatim -- don't rewrite our placements or sizes. Keep everything spot / halftone oriented for screen print -- no CMYK process conversion, no new artwork, no recoloring a design to a different palette.

</details>

<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

The Nocturne Sessions, a fictional indie synth-noir act, is releasing a new EP and needs its launch gig poster finished for print and social. The band has handed off an authored InDesign poster template (nocturne_poster_template.pdf), laid out A2 portrait with a full-bleed hero-photo frame, a wordmark frame, and real InDesign data-merge fields (<<title>>, <<venue>>, <<date>>, <<support>>, <<presale>>). They also supply one raw press photo of the trio (shot on a phone in a dim rehearsal room — slightly tilted, flat/dull, cool white balance, a cluttered gear-strewn background), a flat raster promo wordmark PNG that reads "THE NOCTURNE SESSIONS," and a one-row CSV holding the show copy. The band's brief calls for "a clean modern aesthetic—nothing vintage—powered by bright, bold colours that jump off the screen and still look sharp in print," and the poster's art direction is a classic bold two-tone (duotone) gig-poster look: the hero photo rendered in just two punchy brand inks (deep indigo shadows, hot magenta highlights) rather than full colour, so it reads instantly at both A2 wall size and Instagram thumbnail size. The job: (1) prep the raw press photo — straighten the tilted frame, auto-tone the flat exposure, and push contrast hard so the two-tone mapping has clean separation between shadow and highlight; (2) convert the prepped photo to a bold duotone — first flatten it to a single-ink monochromatic base tint in the indigo shadow ink across the whole frame, then lay the hot-magenta brand ink over it as a whole-image color overlay in a lighten/screen blend so only the brighter pixels shift toward magenta, producing the two-ink poster hero; add a fine grain so the flat inks don't band on large-format print; crop it to the poster frame's ratio; (3) vectorize the flat wordmark PNG into a clean SVG so the "NOCTURNE SESSIONS" word-mark stays razor-sharp at A2 and can be reused on merch/posters exactly as the brief asks; (4) recommend a modern condensed display font pairing for the show copy so the template's type reads as clean and bold; (5) upload the duotoned hero and the vector wordmark, then run the client's authored .indd through InDesign data-merge against the event-copy CSV so the title/venue/date/support/presale bind into the template around the placed hero and wordmark; (6) export the bound poster to a print-ready A2 PDF (300 DPI, CMYK-intent) and a high-resolution JPEG for social. All event copy stays exactly as supplied in the CSV. Deliverables: print-ready PDF, high-res JPEG, the duotone hero PNG, and the wordmark SVG.

</details>

<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

Nordheim Atelier, an independent Scandinavian fashion label, is launching its FW26 'Concrete Season' capsule and needs a poster series finished for its flagship windows and press kit — one A2 portrait poster per runway look, all reading unmistakably as one set. The look is a monochrome documentary-explainer / investigative-magazine aesthetic: isolated cutout photography driven to a warm-toned two-ink editorial duotone, a print-screen halftone dot texture, and a fine film grain so it feels like printed matter, never a cold pure-grey scan. That look is yours to build and to hold identical across every poster; there is no loadable preset and no supplied recipe to lean on — only our one-page mood target (isolated look, warm ink, halftone, grain, consistent across the set). Consistency is the whole job: side by side the six posters must look like the same treatment run on the same day, not six frames each 'fixed' on its own.

We are NOT reshooting. We are handing you six runway captures we already own (full-frame stills, roughly 6000px long edge, sRGB) and here is the problem: they were shot across a moving show under whatever light each moment gave us — some cool and bluish, some warm, one under sickly shop-fluorescent light, one clearly underexposed and one blown a little bright, and a few are tilted a couple of degrees off level. Straight out of the folder they are a mismatched jumble, and once you push a mismatched jumble through the same monochrome treatment the set falls apart — the cool frames go muddy, the bright one goes ghostly, the casts bias the grey conversion differently so no two posters share a tone. To make this checkable we laid a photographic three-patch neutral grey card (light / mid / dark) flat in one corner of every capture. That card is your ground truth. Before you touch the look, bring every capture to a consistent, true-to-neutral base by neutralizing each one to the card it carries: on your corrected frame the three grey patches must read as clean neutral (equal across the channels, no blue / amber / green tint) and the mid patch must sit at the same mid brightness across all six — so the whole set shares one white point and one mid-tone density and the identical duotone lands the same on each. Here is the craft, and it is where a novice fails: the six did NOT start from the same place, so there is no single correction that fixes them. Judge each frame by eye off its own card, work out what is actually wrong with THAT frame, choose the control that clears it, and dial that frame its own move. Do NOT reach for one blanket correction, do NOT copy one frame's numbers onto the rest, and do NOT auto-tone each frame to look fine on its own — auto-tone keys off each frame's own histogram, so the casts will not agree and the set will visibly fail to match at the card. Be careful the other way too: one or more of these may already sit right — if a frame's card already reads neutral and its mid patch is already at target, leave its balance alone; chasing an imagined cast on a frame that is already correct will push it off the set just as badly. And level only the frames that are actually tilted; straightening a level frame throws it off. When you are done, tell us the white-balance and exposure move you applied to each of the six so we can confirm they were reasoned per frame, not eyeballed as one recipe.

Then build the look on the neutralized frames and hold it identical: isolate each look cleanly off its backstage clutter so the garment reads as the hero on a clean plate, drive it to the warm two-ink editorial duotone you author, lay in the halftone print-screen texture and the film grain at the same settings on every look, and crop all six to the template's tall image frame. Our wordmark only exists as a flat scan on off-white paper, slightly crooked with a margin of bare stock around it — get it clean, straight and razor-sharp as a vector so it never looks like a fuzzy scan at poster scale. Finally, assemble the posters: we have hand-built the InDesign poster template with the real placeholder fields and two image slots (one for the treated look, one for the wordmark in the masthead) and we are giving you the roster; merge them so every look gets its own single-page A2 poster with its look number, title and fabric + stylist credit bound in, its treated image dropped into the image frame and the crisp wordmark dropped into the masthead, then hand back one press-ready ~300 DPI A2 PDF covering every look — one page per look. Bind the copy verbatim from the roster; do not rewrite our credits. Acceptance: every grey card neutral and the whole set matched to one white point and one mid density; the duotone / halftone / grain look identical across all six; the wordmark a clean skew-free vector; and exactly one finished poster per roster row.

</details>

We are NOT reshooting. We are handing you eight existing dish photos, and here is the problem: they were shot across a busy service under different light - some under cool fluorescents, some under warm tungsten, a couple under-/over-exposed, on different counters - so straight out of the folder they look like a mismatched jumble, and a storefront of mismatched shots reads cheap. To make this checkable we laid a photographic 18% grey card into the corner of every shot. But do NOT force one blanket correction across the batch - each photo was lit differently and needs its own white-balance, exposure and tone decision to land on the shared target. Be careful: at least one dish is genuinely golden (the baked four-cheese mac is supposed to look deep and warm); if its grey card already reads neutral, do not 'cool' it chasing an imagined blue cast, or you will strip the colour we are selling. Finally, build the tiles: we have hand-built the InDesign tile template with the real placeholder fields and three image slots (background, dish photo, and the wordmark masthead), and we are giving you the menu roster; merge them so every dish gets its own single tile with its copy bound, its matching graded photo dropped in, the backdrop behind it and the crisp wordmark on top, then hand back one press-ready ~300 DPI PDF covering every dish (one tile per dish, the featured pastrami simply among them, page one). Bind the copy verbatim from the roster - do not rewrite our names or prices. Keep it gritty and warm; do not make it clean-corporate. Acceptance: every grey card neutral and the whole set matched to one white point; the backdrop matched to the look; the liner recolour natural under the existing light; the wordmark crisp vector; the hero cleanly on transparency; and exactly one finished tile per roster row.

Kantyna Nova is a modern Polish comfort-food restaurant and catering brand launching a new site and a printed tasting menu, and our food photography has to stop looking like nine unrelated snapshots and start reading as one deliberately-styled brand. We are NOT reshooting. We are handing you nine raw captures straight off a shoot day, and here is the real problem: they were shot in whatever corner of the room was free, so side by side they clash — some came out warm and orange under the tungsten pendants, some cold and blue by the north window, one has a sickly green cast from the old kitchen-pass fluorescents, one is a muddy underexposed mess, one plate is genuinely deep golden-brown and was shot under clean light so it already looks right, and a couple are tilted. Because we knew the light was a mess, our photographer clipped a neutral 18% grey card into the corner of every frame. That card is your ground truth. Job one, cohesion: make the whole set read as ONE set by neutralizing each frame to the grey card it carries — on every graded frame the card must read a clean neutral (no residual warm, blue or green tint) and land on the same mid-grey brightness as the rest, so once every card is neutral the batch shares one white point. Do NOT reach for a single blanket correction, do NOT copy one frame's numbers onto the others, and do NOT auto-tone each frame on its own: each frame was lit differently and a move that rescues one drives another further off, and an auto pass keys off each frame's own histogram so the casts will never agree and the set will visibly fail to match at the cards. Diagnosing what is actually wrong with each frame and choosing the control that clears it is your call, not ours. Be careful with the one plate that is genuinely golden and was shot clean — if its card already reads neutral, do not 'cool' it chasing a cast that is not there, or you will strip the real color of the food. When you are done, tell us the white-balance and exposure move you settled on for each frame so we can confirm they were matched to the cards, not eyeballed. The house look itself — a warm, rich, premium restaurant tone with lifted shadows, gentle contrast, the crispness that makes crumb and glaze and steam read, and a restrained pop so the food looks appetizing without going garish or plastic — is yours to build and hold identical across all nine; there is no preset to load, only our one-page look note. Job two, make the food the hero, but use judgement: several plates were shot on cluttered tables and the busy background fights the dish, so the dish needs to be lifted off its surroundings — but some plates were already shot clean, and two of these captures are overhead spreads where the whole surface IS the subject and there is no single hero to isolate. Treat each shot as it needs and leave the ones that are already working alone; getting that wrong quietly ruins a shot and nobody notices until it prints. Keep everything natural — no over-processing. Deliverables: (1) the nine graded masters as a contact set our marketing lead can eyeball against the cards; (2) a press-ready printed tasting menu, one dish per page, built from our menu copy and our InDesign menu template with each graded dish photo dropped in, exported as a single print PDF; (3) an authored monochrome cover treatment of the dining-room ambience shot for the menu cover and the site header; (4) a matched web hero set of the catering spread for the site landing. Brand direction: warm, rich, premium, appetizing; consistent across every image; natural, not garish.

</details>

<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

SlabVault Cards runs an online consignment storefront for graded sports-card slabs, and we need this new-intake batch turned into a clean, uniform set plus a printed consignment comp-card for each slab. Here is the honest situation with the photos: the owner shot all six slabs on an iPhone at the kitchen table, but across two sittings — a few in the morning by the window (they come out cold and slightly blue), the rest that evening under the warm work-lamp (they come out orange), and one under the greenish overhead in the back room. So straight out of the folder the six look like they were shot by three different people: the same white slab case reads blue in one and amber in another, some are dull and underexposed, one is a touch blown out. A storefront grid where every slab has a different colour cast looks amateur and kills buyer trust on items worth real money. To give you an honest reference we laid a photographic 18% grey card at the edge of every shot. What we need on the photos: bring all six to one consistent, true look by neutralizing each frame to the grey card it contains, so once every card reads a clean neutral the whole set sits at one shared white point and one exposure feel. Do NOT push one blanket correction across all six — each sitting was lit differently and some frames need warming while others need cooling, and forcing the same numbers through all of them will leave the set mismatched. When you are done, tell us the final white-balance and exposure move you landed on for each frame so we can trust the set is genuinely matched and not just eyeballed. Then lift each slab cleanly off the cluttered table — the wood grain, the charger cable, the coffee ring and the grey card must all be gone — and set it on flat pure-white (#FFFFFF), no drop shadow, no grey gradient, just clean white the way the storefront wants. This part has a hard consistency rule the last freelancer missed: every slab must sit at the SAME scale in its frame with even margin, so a small vintage slab and a tall modern slab do not jump size-to-size down the grid; and each finished slab image has to carry enough real pixels to print sharp inside the comp-card photo window — a slab cropped down to a little web thumbnail will print soft and we will reject it. Second, the grading-partner seals: two of our graders' marks go on the cards depending on who graded the slab — the GRADEX seal is a flat printed two-colour logo, and the APEX seal is a photograph of the graders' holographic tamper-proof authentication hologram, all sheen and rainbow gradient. Both need to be prepped so they drop cleanly into the card's seal window and stay sharp at print size — but they are not the same kind of file and should not be handled the same way; think about which one can honestly become clean line art and which one cannot survive that. Finally, build the cards: we have hand-built the InDesign consignment comp-card template with the real placeholder fields and two image slots (the slab photo and the grading seal), and we are giving you the consignment roster; merge them so every slab gets its own single comp-card with the player, set/year, grade, cert number and ask price bound in verbatim from the roster, its cleaned slab photo dropped into the photo window, and its grading-partner seal in the seal window — then hand back a press-ready ~300 DPI PDF, one comp-card per slab. Do not invent or reassign any slab's details; bind them verbatim. Acceptance: every grey card neutral and the whole set on one white point (with your per-frame WB/exposure move reported); every slab on flat pure-white at one consistent fill-scale with even margin and enough resolution to print >=300 DPI in the photo window; the two grading seals each prepped the correct way and razor-sharp at print size; and exactly one finished comp-card per roster row.

</details>

Marisol Cove is a fictional boutique clifftop hotel on a sun-washed clifftop coast, rebuilding its homepage. The new homepage runs as six stacked full-width section bands — Stays, Weddings, Coastline, Spa, Dining and Contact — each with its own hero banner behind the headline, and the whole page has to read as ONE room: one light, one warmth, one premium mood, top to bottom. We do NOT have our own photography yet and we do NOT need the website built here — our developer handles the build. What we need is the hero imagery, finished and cohesive, plus a proof book we can sign off in the founders' meeting. Please source our heroes from a stock library: we want three high-resolution widescreen coastal shots — turquoise sea, whitewashed clifftop villas with terracotta roofs, white terrace parasols, generous open sky — each large enough that you can crop two different section banners out of it without ever enlarging it. Here is the catch, and it is the whole job: stock shots of the same coastline are taken at different times of day under different light, so out of the box they will NOT match — one will feel warm and amber, one cool and overcast, one shot straight into a golden sunset. If we drop three mismatched images down the page it looks cheap and broken. Your job is to bring all three to our single house 'warm-coastal' look — a soft, sun-warmed, premium feel where the whitewashed villa walls read as one consistent warm-white across all three images and the deep shade under the cliffs sits at one consistent soft near-black (deep, not crushed to dead black, never a clipped channel). Because the three start from different light, matching the OUTPUT means each needs a DIFFERENT correction: some want warming, some want cooling, some want an exposure lift and some a pull-down — pushing the same slider settings through all three will leave the page mismatched, and we will reject it. Be careful with the sunset frame in particular: judge it on its own walls, not on the instruction to 'make it golden' — if its walls already read as our warm-white, warming it further to chase the sunset will push it off the set. When you are done, hand us a short sheet listing, per source, the white-balance and exposure moves you dialed, so we can confirm the three were matched to one target and not just each 'auto-fixed' to look fine alone. From the three graded masters, cut our six section heroes: a wide cinematic band for the full-width sections (Stays, Coastline, Dining) and a taller framing for the feature sections (Weddings, Spa, Contact), each leaving clear open sky or open water on one side so our headline has room to breathe — do not let the buildings crowd the copy zone. One more thing about size, and it matters: those six section banners are web-sized, for our developer's live site. But the proof book we sign off prints FULL-BLEED at A4 landscape, so each section's hero also has to reach that page at true print resolution, filling the whole trim edge to edge at around 300 DPI. We refuse anything upscaled — so that print-sized hero has to be cut DOWN from the big stock source too, exactly like the web banners, never blown up from a web crop. So give us, per section, TWO cuts from the same graded master: a print-resolution hero that fills the full-bleed proof page as a genuine downscale, and a web-sized banner for the site. Next, our two brand marks, which are NOT the same kind of file and must not be treated the same: (1) our wordmark, a flat cream 'MARISOL COVE' lockup we are handing you as a slightly skewed scan on off-white paper — get it clean, straight and razor-sharp as crisp line art for every section masthead; (2) our founder's seal, the small embossed brass 'EST. MMXIX' medallion, which we are handing you as a close-up PHOTOGRAPH with all its metallic sheen and relief — it has to drop onto the pages with its shine intact and must NOT be turned into flat line art. Think about which mark can become vector and which one cannot survive it. Finally, assemble the proof: we have hand-built the section-proof layout template (a genuine authored .indd/.idml) with the real placeholder fields and three image slots (the section hero, the wordmark masthead, and the seal), and we are giving you the six-section roster with our headlines and sub-heads; merge them so every section gets its own proof page with its copy bound, its matching graded print-resolution hero placed full-bleed, the crisp wordmark in the masthead and the seal in the corner — then hand back one press-ready ~300 DPI A4-landscape PDF proof book covering all six sections, one section per page, for the sign-off deck. Bind our headlines and sub-heads verbatim from the roster; do not rewrite our copy. Acceptance: all three sources matched to one warm-coastal white point and one soft-black on their whitewashed-wall and cliff-shadow references; six section heroes cut from them with clean copy space and no upscaling anywhere — each section's full-bleed proof hero a genuine downscale from the large source landing at ~300 DPI at the page trim, distinct from the web-sized banner; the two marks prepped the correct way (one crisp vector, one transparent-ground raster with its sheen intact); and exactly one proof page per roster section.

</details>

<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

Harbor Crest Realty is a fictional boutique waterfront-and-city brokerage refreshing both its website imagery and its printed listing leave-behind. Our site structure and copy already work; the imagery feels dated and mismatched and no longer signals the premium, trustworthy feel we want. We are NOT building the website here — our developer handles the build — we need the finished, cohesive imagery plus a listings proof book we can sign off in a partners' meeting. The whole thing has to read as ONE brand: one light, one warmth, one premium mood, top to bottom.

FIRST, our own listing photography. We are handing you six photos our agents shot across six different homes over the last month (roughly 4000px, straight off the camera). They do NOT match: every room was lit by whatever was there — warm ceiling downlights, a cool north-facing window, old kitchen fluorescents, a mixed window-and-lamp split, one dim twilight exterior, one exterior caught in strong late light. Because we knew the light was a mess, our photographer clipped a neutral grey balance card (a mid-grey patch beside a white patch) into every frame. Use that card as your ground truth: every listing photo has to be neutralised so the card reads truly neutral — no residual warm, blue or green cast — and so the card's mid-grey sits at the same brightness across all six, then carried to ONE Harbor Crest house look: clean, warm-but-not-orange, shadows open so interiors read airy, whites held so windows keep detail, a restrained premium pop. Here is the craft, and it is where our last editor failed: the six did NOT start from the same place, so there is no single correction that fixes them — a move that rescues one frame drives another further off. Judge each frame by eye off its own card, work out what is actually wrong with THAT frame, choose the right control to neutralise it, and dial that frame its own correction until all six cards land on the same neutral and the same mid-grey. Do NOT reach for one global white-balance number, do NOT copy one frame's settings onto the others, and do NOT just auto-tone each one to look fine alone — auto-tone keys off each frame's own histogram, so the casts will not agree and the set will visibly fail to match at the card, and we will reject it. And read each frame honestly: if a frame already reads on our warm house look, do not push it further to chase a mood — match it to the set, do not overcook it. The look itself is yours to build from scratch and hold identical across the set; there is no preset to lean on, only our one-page house-look target (neutral card + whites-held + open shadows + gentle contrast + restrained warmth).

SECOND, the website hero imagery. We do not have a wide, aspirational hero shot of our own, so license one from Adobe Stock: a high-quality modern light-filled living space or a clean contemporary home exterior in warm natural light, no recognisable faces, no readable signage, and licensed LARGE — big enough (roughly 5000px on the long edge) that you can cut several web slots out of it without ever enlarging it. That stock hero has to belong to the same family as our listings, so match-grade it to the SAME house white point you established on the listing batch — but the stock frame has no grey card, so judge it on its own natural neutral (the white trim, white cabinetry or white parasols in the shot) until it sits on the same warm-white as the set. From that one graded master, cut our web slots, each perfectly sized for its destination and each framed so the architecture survives the reframe: a desktop hero 2560x1080, a tablet hero 1536x1024, a mobile hero 1080x1350, two low-band section-header strips 1920x480 for the 'Featured Listings' and 'About Us' sections, a leaderboard promo banner 1200x628, and a square promo 1080x1080 — and give the square one a subtle navy monochromatic treatment so it reads as the stylised promo variant rather than a plain photo. Every one of those is cut DOWN from the big licensed master — never stretched, never AI-expanded.

THIRD, our two brand marks, which are NOT the same kind of file and must not be treated the same. We are handing you two of them. One can become clean, razor-sharp vector line art for every masthead and print corner; the other cannot survive being turned into flat line art and has to stay a photographic raster with its real surface intact. Work out which is which, prep each the right way, and hand back the vector as an SVG and the raster as a transparent-background PNG. (One of them will need straightening and cleaning before it can be traced at all — do not trace it raw.)

FOURTH, the sign-off artifact. We have hand-built the featured-listings card template (a genuine authored .indd) with live placeholder fields and three image slots — the listing photo, the wordmark masthead and the corner seal — and we are giving you the six-listing roster with our addresses, prices and headline copy. Merge them so every listing gets its own proof page with its copy bound, its matching graded photo placed, the crisp vector wordmark in the masthead and the seal in the corner, then hand back one press-ready featured-listings proof book, one listing per page, for the partners' deck. Bind our copy verbatim from the roster; do not rewrite it. Finally, recommend an on-brand heading/label typeface pairing for the mini style reference.

Deliverables: the six graded listing masters (as a contact set we can eyeball against the card), the graded stock hero master, the responsive web set (desktop/tablet/mobile heroes, two section headers, leaderboard + navy square banner), the wordmark SVG and the seal PNG prepped the correct way each, the font-pairing note, the press-ready featured-listings proof book (one listing per page), and a short note listing the final white-balance and exposure move you applied to each of the six listing photos and to the stock hero — so we can confirm the set was matched to the card, not just eyeballed. Everything must feel part of one family.

</details>

To feed that merge, isolate the broker cleanly from his studio backdrop as a transparent figure, and clean our wordmark (it only exists as a flat raster) into a razor-sharp vector so it prints crisp at any size on the sheet.

- A flat PNG of the channel wordmark lockup ('HALDEN', with the tagline and a small play glyph).
- One ~12s 4K episode take (episode_take_4k.mp4) for the social reframe.
- My channel's episode style-frame sheet layout (halden_episode_sheet.indd) and this week's episode list (episode_kit.csv): eight rows, the episode number, episode title, air date and the segment tag for each, plus the image slots.

What I need back:
- THE EPISODE STYLE-FRAME SHEET (the main deliverable): a press-ready ~300 DPI PDF of my per-episode brand sheet, ONE episode per page, eight pages, that I keep as the channel's reference and hand to my editor so lower-thirds and end screens sit on the same look every week. Each page binds its episode number, title, air date and segment tag from the list, drops that episode's graded hero still into the sheet's hero window, and carries my wordmark crisp in the masthead.
- THE LOOK (this is the whole craft): the eight sheet pages have to read as ONE channel, not eight stills from eight different days. Bring every still to the SAME house look — a warm, personal, upbeat grade that is nonetheless consistent frame to frame. Use the grey card in each still to get them all onto ONE common house white point and one shared exposure feel first: because every still started in different light, how far and which way you move is a per-still decision you judge off that still's own card — a batch that is each 'auto-fixed' to look fine on its own will drift apart at the grey cards and I will send it back. Then put my house character on all eight the same way — the warm, lifted, lively feel the channel is known for. Keep skin natural, not orange; keep it lively, not garish. When you are done, hand me, per still, the white-balance (temperature/tint) and exposure move you dialed and the final pixel size, so I can trust the set was matched to one target rather than eyeballed one at a time.
- THE THUMBNAIL: from the hero episode's graded still, give me a clean channel thumbnail at 1280x720 with me clearly popped off the busy room behind me (the background knocked back so I read first).
- THE VERTICAL COVER: from that same popped hero still, a vertical story/cover at 1080x1920, reframed from the existing pixels only — no re-shoot, no invented canvas.
- THE WORDMARK: my flat wordmark cleaned to a crisp, infinitely-scalable vector so it stays razor-sharp in lower-thirds and on the end screen at any size, and reusable across future episodes.
- THE SOCIAL REFRAME: the ~12s 4K episode take reframed to a same-length 1080x1920 vertical for the story feed — no trimming, no re-cut, just the vertical reframe.

PRINT SIZE: each sheet page drops the hero still into a 190 x 107 mm (16:9) hero window, which at press resolution needs at least ~2244 x 1264 px of real image; the stills are full-resolution camera frames, so a 16:9 crop from the full frame clears that — do not grade on a small proxy or enlarge past what the frame holds. Acceptance: every grey card matched to one common house white point across all eight with the per-still moves reported; the same authored house look on all eight; the thumbnail exactly 1280x720 with the background knocked back; the cover exactly 1080x1920 from existing pixels; the wordmark a crisp vector on every masthead; the reframe exactly 1080x1920 at the take's full runtime; and exactly one sheet page per episode-list row.

</details>

<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

Norvant is launching a 90-second informative explainer about our workflow-automation platform and we need the whole launch kit built from the raw material we're sending. Here is what you get and what we need back.

Raw material: ONE long continuous UHD recording — about three and a half minutes, shot in a single sitting of our founder talking to camera at her desk with a laptop showing our dashboard. We shot it as one take on purpose and let the room light change through the session: it opens under our warm desk tungsten, we opened the blinds to cool daylight partway through for the dashboard talk, and by the end the low golden-hour sun was raking warm across the desk. So the same take carries a few different looks depending on where you pull from it. On the edge of the desk we clipped a neutral 18% grey card and a small white chip, in frame for the whole take, so the stills can be balanced honestly after the fact. The audio has some steady room hiss. You also get our wordmark, which unfortunately only exists as a slightly crooked desktop scan on off-white paper, a loose narrative outline, and a short CSV of the exact on-screen copy for our launch cards (headlines, the two lower-third names/roles, the call-out stat, the end-card call to action) — bind that copy verbatim, do not rewrite it.

VIDEO: from that one recording we need three things. First, clean the room hiss off the audio. Second, give us a punchy ~90-second highlight cut of the take that surfaces the key points — it's a highlight pulled from the longer recording, not something stitched together or stretched out. Third, give us a same-length 9:16 vertical version for social — same length as the highlight, no trimming. We're not asking for burned-in captions or motion graphics — just the clean cut and the vertical.

POSTER FRAMES — the heart of the colour job: pull six stills from the take to use as the imagery in the launch cards — one hero moment for the title card, two moments for the lower-thirds, one for the stat call-out, one for the section divider, one for the end card. Because the light shifted across the take, straight out of the recording these six stills do NOT match — some read warm, some cool, one is a genuinely golden close. We need all six to look like ONE piece, one house look, as if they were the same shot: balance each one honestly using the grey card we clipped in frame so they share one neutral white point, floor the darks at one shared level (deep but never crushed to solid black), and carry the same appetising, slightly filmic tonality across all six — lifted shadows, protected highlights, a little clarity. They need to read as one continuous set, not six separately-tweaked stills. One thing we care about: where a moment is genuinely warm because the light really was that warm, that mood is intentional — keep the natural life in it, don't drain it grey. On the hero title-card frame, lift the founder off the background so she reads cleanly with room on one side for the headline. When you're done, tell us the white-balance and exposure you landed on for each of the six frames so we can confirm the set is matched.

WORDMARK: get our scanned wordmark clean and razor-sharp as vector art for the cards — it must not look like a fuzzy, crooked scan when it prints.

LAUNCH CARDS: we've hand-built the InDesign card template with the real placeholder fields and an image slot, and we're giving you the copy CSV. Merge them so every launch card — title, the two lower-thirds, the stat call-out, the section divider, the end card — comes out as its own finished page with its copy set in type, its matched poster frame placed, and the vector wordmark in the corner. Hand back one press-ready ~300 DPI PDF, one card per row, plus the six matched frames and the vector logo, all organised so we can tweak later. Acceptance: interview audio noticeably cleaner; a ~90s highlight and a same-length 9:16; every grey card neutral at one shared white point with the darks floored at one shared level; the intentional warmth of the naturally-warm moments kept; the wordmark a crisp skew-free vector; and exactly one finished card per CSV row. Two rounds of feedback should be plenty.

</details>

<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

Milepost Driving Academy is standing up a learner-guide system: a printed and on-screen card for every core driving scenario (four-way stop, roundabout entry, lane merge, pedestrian crossing, T-junction, parallel-parking bay), plus a small library of reusable road-sign vector art and a vertical clip for the phone feed. We are NOT asking you to animate anything — our own artist handles motion. We need the source-asset craft and the finished card set.

Here is what you are given and the problem with it. Our photographer spent a day capturing one clean reference still at each scenario, but the light kept changing through the day, so straight out of the folder the six shots look like they belong to six different guides, and a learner flipping through cards that do not match reads as sloppy. On every frame the photographer left a photographic 18% grey card in shot (clipped to a post or laid at the kerb) so you have an honest neutral reference to balance against. Job one: bring all six to ONE house look — the grey card in each frame must read as a clean neutral, and once the set is balanced it must share a single white point and one consistent brightness, so a learner cannot tell which time of day any card was shot. Judge each frame on its OWN grey card rather than assuming they all drifted the same way — some sit closer to neutral than others, and over-correcting a frame is as wrong as under-correcting it. Keep the retained reference frames (grey card still in shot) so we can confirm each one actually landed neutral, and give us a SEPARATE set with the card cropped out for the cards themselves. When you are done, tell us, per frame, the white-balance and exposure you landed on, so we can trust the set is matched and not eyeballed.

Job two, the sign art. We are sending two things that both concern signage: (a) a flat, drawn sign-glyph sheet on a plain white ground (stop, give-way, pedestrian, roundabout, no-entry, speed roundel), which we want turned into clean scalable vector art for the card library; and (b) one real photograph of a give-way sign on a metal pole against sky, shot slightly off-square, which we also want as a clean vector of the SIGN ONLY. We need both as crisp closed vector shapes with no captured sky, pole, background or skew baked in — handle each input in whatever way gets it there cleanly.

Job three, the clip. We shot one dashcam pass approaching a junction, landscape, and want a same-length vertical version for the phone feed plus one representative still lifted from it to sit on the guide as the cover image — bring that cover still to the same house look as the six scenario frames so it belongs to the set.

Job four, the cards. We have hand-built the InDesign learner-card template with the real placeholder fields and an image slot, and we are giving you the scenario roster. Merge them so every scenario gets its own single card with its title, the what-to-do steps, the common-mistake line and the caption bound from the roster, and its matched scenario photo dropped into the image frame. Bind our copy verbatim — do not rewrite the guidance. Hand back one press-ready ~300 DPI card set (one page per scenario) AND a screen-optimised version of the same set. Recommend a clean, legible typeface for the card body that sits with our wordmark.

Acceptance: every grey card neutral and the six matched to one white point (with your per-frame parameters reported, confirmed on the retained card-bearing reference frames), plus the card-cropped scenario set with the reference card removed; both sign inputs delivered as clean skew-free vectors with no background captured; the vertical clip the same length as the source; and exactly one finished card per roster row.

</details>

The catch is that the six start from completely different lighting, so getting all six to sit together as one set — matched at that concrete and matched down in the shadows — is the whole job. We judge the grid as a WHOLE: six frames that each look fine on their own but don't read as the same room are exactly what we reject.

2) An A/B HERO-THUMBNAIL SET. From the best of the pulled frames, give us TWO thumbnails that are two genuinely DIFFERENT art directions we can split-test — not the same look twice. Direction A is loud clickbait energy: bright, punchy, high-contrast, warm and saturated. Direction B is a moody cinematic treatment: pulled-down and desaturated with cool teal shadows. Both 1280x720, both composed with the subject to one side so we can drop our own title text into the open space later (do NOT add text yourself).

3) Reusable brand overlays. Both brand graphics need prepping so we can reuse them everywhere. The EMBLEM is our channel mark — it rides as a small corner watermark on every video and blows up big on the end-card, so it has to stay pin-sharp at every size, from tiny bug to full-screen, with no soft edges or jaggies ever. The MASCOT we want to be able to drop onto anything — thumbnails, end-cards, panels — sitting cleanly on top of whatever is behind it, with none of its own background clinging to it. Prep each one into the form its job needs.

4) The upload cuts. Clean up the commentary on the primary clip so the voice is clear, and give us three platform reframes of that clip at the SAME length (no re-timing): the 16:9 master, a 9:16 vertical for Shorts, and a 1:1 square.

<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

I run @nightform, a fast-growing vertical short-video account, and I need one night-drive shoot turned into a post-ready drop package. I am NOT looking for a finished timeline film here — my editor does the final cut, the caption burn-in and any motion graphics on the timeline. What I need from you is the colour and cover package built off the ONE take we already shot.

Here is what you get: (1) nightdrive_take_4k.mp4 — a single continuous ~45 second 4K night-drive take, hand-held-steady from inside the car: pulling away from a lit kerb, rolling under a concrete underpass, stopped at a lit crossing, out across a wet open stretch, past a strip of neon storefronts, and finally around a lamp-lit off-ramp. Because it is one long take through changing street light, different moments do NOT match each other straight out of the file — some are warm and dim, some go cold and murky, some are blown out with neon. To make the match checkable we clipped an 18% grey card to the dashboard at the edge of frame and it stays in shot the whole take. (2) coverboard_template.indd — the cover-card page we hand-built, one card per page, with the real placeholder fields and two image slots (the full-bleed cover and the corner wordmark lockup). (3) cover_shotlist.csv — our six-beat list: the beat name, a framing note, a run label and a format tag per card. (4) nightform_wordmark_flat.png — our flat wordmark on transparency, which we want razor-sharp in the corner of every cover. (5) captions_script.json — a short caption cue-sheet.

What I need back:
- THE COVER BOARD (the deliverable I care about most): a designed cover board, ONE cover card per beat, six cards, that I review and post from. For each of the six beats, pull the strongest, SHARP frame near that beat out of the take (if the beat lands on a motion-blurred moment, step to the clean frame beside it — a soft cover reads cheap and I will reject it), grade it, drop it full-bleed into the card with its beat name, run label and my @nightform handle bound in from the list, and my wordmark crisp in the corner lockup. The cover has to look art-directed, not like a filter dropped on a screenshot.
- THE GRADE (this is the whole craft of it): the six cards have to read as ONE drop, not six frames from six different nights. First bring every pulled frame to the SAME neutral base — the grey card in that frame has to land truly neutral (no leftover warm or cold cast) at one common white point, and the set has to share one exposure feel. Because the take's light drifts, no two beats start from the same cast or brightness, so getting all six onto that one white point is a per-frame decision — each frame gets neutralized to its OWN in-frame grey card, and how far and which way to move is yours to judge from that card, frame by frame. A set that is each 'auto-fixed' to look fine on its own will drift apart at the grey cards and I will reject it. THEN put them all onto one night-look I can call mine: cool and moody with the blacks set deep, the harsh street-light colours settled back so they don't fight the mood, and the neon accent given a controlled lift — one look, built to my brand, applied so all six covers feel like one release. Judge the look per frame too: a frame swamped by one street-light colour needs a heavier hand than one already close, or the set won't match. When you are done, hand back, per frame, the white-balance (temperature / tint) and exposure move you dialed and the final pixel size, so I can confirm the set was matched to one target rather than eyeballed.
- COVER SIZE: each cover card is a 1080 x 1920 vertical, and the cover image behind it needs to fill that at full 1080 x 1920 from real pixels — the take is 4K, so a vertical crop from the full frame clears it; a cover graded on a small proxy, or a landscape frame stretched to fill vertical, will fall under and post soft. Do not enlarge past what the 4K frame holds.
- THE REEL: a ~15 second vertical (1080x1920) sizzle cut from the SAME take for the drop — shortened from the long take (no lengthening, no stitching in other clips) and reframed to vertical, no upscaling (the 4K master has the height for it). Frame-accurate timeline cuts, transitions, motion graphics and burned-in captions are my editor's timeline finish, not part of this pass.
- THE WORDMARK: my flat wordmark cleaned to a crisp vector for the corner lockup and reusable on future covers.
- THE CAPTIONS: my caption cue-sheet finalized into the project folder as a data asset for my editor to burn on during the timeline finish — I know the automated pass doesn't paint text onto the video.

Keep the sources in my cloud project folder. Bind the beat names, run labels and my handle verbatim from the list — do not rename my beats.
