<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

Anvil & Oak Strength Co. is building a printed movement-library card deck for our coaching floor and client handouts: one clean reference card per core exercise, each carrying the movement name, the primary and secondary muscles worked, two or three form cues, the tempo, and a common-fault line, with a strong demo photo of the coach mid-movement, our wordmark at the top, and our certification seal on the card. We are NOT asking you to add captions, arrows, or graphics onto the videos — our floor coaches handle any on-screen teaching in their own tools. We need the source-asset craft and the finished card set, built to print.

Here is what you are given and the problem with it. We filmed six core movements — Goblet Squat, Romanian Deadlift, Push-Up, Bent-Over Row, Overhead Press, Walking Lunge — one continuous demo take each, shot on six different days in whichever corner of the studio was free, so the light is all over the place: one under warm tungsten work-lights, one by a cool north window, one under greenish overhead fluorescents, and so on, and a couple are framed a few degrees off level. Each take is a real two-to-three-minute recording of the coach talking through and demonstrating the movement, with restarts, resets between reps and dead air around the strong reps. On the mat at the edge of frame we left an 18% grey reference card in shot for the whole of every take, so white balance can be reconciled after the fact.

What we need back, and the bar it has to clear:

1) PER MOVEMENT, one short landscape highlight — the strongest, most watchable stretch of that movement's demo take cut down to roughly fifteen seconds with the resets and dead air dropped, sixteen-by-nine, for our socials and our app's exercise page. Each highlight comes from that one movement's take only.

2) PER MOVEMENT, one hero POSTER FRAME lifted from the demo take — a sharp, in-focus frame at the working position of the lift (the loaded bottom of the squat, the hinge of the deadlift, and so on) with the coach's whole working body in frame and the grey card visible — then all six graded so the deck reads as ONE studio look. Every frame's grey reference card must read a clean neutral (no residual warm or cool cast) at one common white point, the whole set sharing one deep black floor, skin kept natural and any bright window not blown. The six were shot on different days under different light, so getting all six to sit at one white point at the grey card is the whole job — a deck whose cards each drift a different colour reads cheap and we will reject it. Do NOT push one blanket correction across all six: each needs its own white-balance and exposure decision, and at least one of them was already shot under good neutral light and should be left where it is rather than 'corrected' to match an imagined cast. Hand back, per movement, the retained card-bearing neutralized master with the grey card still in frame as your neutrality proof; then crop the grey card out for the card's photo window. These are going to print at A5, so each poster crop must hold enough real pixels to print sharp at ~300 DPI in the card's photo window — a frame cropped down small will print soft and we will reject it. When you are done, tell us, per movement, the white-balance (temperature/tint), exposure and black point you dialed, so we can confirm the set was matched to one target and not eyeballed.

3) OUR TWO BRAND MARKS, print-ready for the cards. The first is our wordmark, which only exists as a flat scan on off-white paper, slightly crooked on the scan bed — clean it up and make it crisp scalable art for the card header. The second is our certification seal, which we are giving you as a close-up photograph of the physical embossed pressed-metal coin, with its raised lettering, metal sheen and the soft shadows in the emboss. Both need to drop cleanly onto the cards and stay sharp at print size — but they are not the same kind of file and must not be treated the same way: think about which one can honestly become flat line art and which one would be destroyed by that.

4) BUILD THE DECK. We have hand-built the InDesign exercise-card template with the real placeholder fields and three image slots (the demo photo, the wordmark header, the seal), and we are giving you the movement roster. Merge them so every movement gets its own single card with its name, muscles, cues, tempo and common-fault line bound in, its matched graded poster dropped into the photo window, the crisp wordmark in the header and the seal on the card — then hand back one press-ready ~300 DPI A5 PDF, one card per movement. Bind our copy verbatim from the roster — do not rewrite our cues or reassign muscles. Recommend a clean, legible body typeface that sits with our wordmark.

Acceptance: every grey card neutral and the six matched to one white point and one black floor (with your per-movement parameters reported, confirmed on the retained card-bearing masters), plus the card-cropped poster set with the grey card removed and each holding enough pixels to print sharp at A5; the wordmark a clean skew-free vector and the seal a high-res transparent raster with its emboss intact; each highlight a single-clip shorten of its own take; and exactly one finished reference card per roster row.

</details>

We are FOLD & GRAIN, a small packaging design studio, and we are launching a new website and refreshing the leave-behind one-sheet we hand to prospective clients after a pitch. Because the shelf is lit by mixed sources and the light changes along its length, the six projects do NOT sit under matching light in the take: some frames come out warm, some cool, some darker, some flat. So we could photograph a reference: a photographic 18% grey card sits in each project's framing, under that project's own light, and stays in shot. (2) portfolio_board_template.indd — the one-project-per-page portfolio-board page we hand-built, with the live placeholder fields and two image slots (the project frame and the masthead). (3) project_list.csv — our six-project run list: the project name, the material, the client sector, a format tag and the approximate position of that project in the take, one row per project. (4) foldgrain_wordmark_flat.png — our flat studio wordmark on transparency, which we want razor-sharp on the board masthead.

What we need back:
- THE SIZZLE (hero video): a fast, energetic short cut off the one take for the top of the homepage, and a full-length vertical (1080x1920) version of the same take for social — same footage, reframed tall, no trimming and no upscaling (the take is 4K, so it has the height for vertical).
- THE PORTFOLIO BOARD (the main print deliverable, and the real craft): a press-ready ~300 DPI PDF of our leave-behind one-sheet, ONE project per page, six pages, that our print vendor runs. For each project on the run list, pull the SINGLE strongest, SHARP frame of that project out of the take (if the position we noted lands on a motion-blurred moment in the move, step to the clean frame beside it — a soft frame prints muddy and we will reject it), grade it, and drop it into the page's project window with its project name, material, sector and format tag bound in from the run list, and our wordmark crisp in the masthead.
- THE GRADE (this is the whole point): the board and the sizzle have to read as ONE studio's work, not six frames grabbed from six different lighting positions. Bring every pulled frame to the SAME house look — a clean, true grade where the neutral grey card in that frame lands truly neutral (no leftover warm or cool cast) at one common white point, and the set shares one exposure feel. Because the shelf light drifts, no two frames start from the same cast or brightness, so getting all six onto that one white point is a per-frame decision — each frame has to be neutralized to its OWN in-frame grey card, and how far and which way to move is yours to judge from that card, frame by frame. A set that is each 'auto-fixed' to look fine on its own will drift apart at the grey cards and we will reject it. Keep the printed package artwork punchy but not blown; neutral, not cast. When you are done, hand back, per frame, the white-balance (temperature / tint) and exposure move you dialed and the final pixel size, so we can confirm the set was matched to one target rather than eyeballed frame by frame.

- THE WORDMARK: our flat wordmark cleaned to a crisp vector for the board masthead and reusable on future covers.

Keep the sources in our shared cloud folder. Bind the project names, materials, sectors and tags verbatim from the run list — do not rename our projects. We shot on two cameras under two lighting setups that do NOT match out of camera: the host desk runs warm off our tungsten key (orange cast, a touch dark), the product table runs cool off the window daylight (blue cast, a touch bright), and the verdict take at the desk came out warm AND brighter than the intro. On every camera we keep a small neutral grey + white reference card clipped just inside the frame edge so you have something honest to balance against.

What we need back is the whole publish package, and it has to be genuinely on-brand, not just exported:

(1) A short-form highlight cut of the episode for Shorts/Reels -- pull the strongest ~30-50 seconds of hook and verdict out of the long-form master. Clean up the host's narration on that short so it sits clear over the room tone. Then give us that same short reframed two ways: a full vertical 9:16 and a square 1:1, both keeping the host and the phone in frame.

(2) A thumbnail pack, and this is where channels usually fall apart: we want one 16:9 thumbnail (our main grid tile), one 1:1, and one 9:16 story tile, each built from a clean hero still off a DIFFERENT scene of the episode -- but all three have to read as the SAME channel. That means every still neutralised to its own grey card and then carried to ONE Voltcast house look: a slightly cool, punchy, contrast-forward grade with a deep-but-not-crushed black. The three stills start from opposite casts and different exposures (a warm-ish dark desk, a cool-ish bright table, and a brighter warm verdict), so getting them all to land on the same house look is the whole job -- figure out what each frame needs on its own to reach the shared target. A pack where each still was just 'auto-fixed' to look fine on its own will read like three different shows in the grid, and we will send it back. Keep skin tones believable on the host and don't blow the phone screens or the specular on the glass. Crop the reference card out of every finished thumbnail.

(3) Our channel bug (the little Voltcast wordmark + bolt glyph) cleaned to a transparent PNG and vectorized to a crisp SVG so it stays sharp as the corner bug on the dark player and on retina.

Hard rules: this is a package build, NOT a re-edit -- do not promise timeline trims to exact timestamps, motion graphics, or burned-in text; we know the tooling doesn't do that. Let the highlight tool choose the cut, clean the speech on the cut, reframe the cleaned cut, and pull your thumbnail stills from the scene selects. Deliver the short + its 9:16 and 1:1 reframes, the three matched thumbnails, and the vector bug. <details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

SentinelMesh is a B2B AI-powered cybersecurity platform that reduces human cyber risk through real-time protection, adaptive phishing simulations, and in-the-moment coaching. We're preparing a funding round and a website refresh and need a launch-collateral package: a product-demo video with social cutdowns, a matched set of product stills, and a printable per-claim feature-card set for the sales binder and investor leave-behind. The pieces run on our website hero, in sales decks, webinars, investor discussions, and across LinkedIn / X.

What we're supplying: (1) two 1080p screen-capture recordings of the SentinelMesh console — the real-time threat dashboard and the adaptive-simulation builder; (2) two short b-roll clips of the product running on a laptop in a modern office (a primary take plus supplemental coverage from another angle) so there is real, cuttable footage; (3) FIVE full-resolution product stills — the console on a laptop by a window, the console in a meeting room, a dark-mode beauty shot of the dashboard, a wide security-operations-room frame, and a close on the in-the-moment coaching nudge — shot across two sessions under mismatched light, each with a photographic 18% grey card laid at the edge of the frame as a neutral reference so white balance can be reconciled honestly after the fact; (4) our logo two ways — a flat, crisp vector-style PNG, and a second copy photographed as printed office signage (real lighting, paper texture, a slight cast); (5) a messaging matrix CSV distilled from our whitepapers holding the key claims in priority order with a proof point and a call-to-action for each, plus a column naming which product still supports each claim; and (6) our hand-built InDesign feature-card template with live placeholder fields and an image slot.

What we need back:

A. VIDEO. Assemble the raw recordings and b-roll into one polished product-demo MASTER — the longest of the three pieces — then a shorter promotional cutdown and a shorter-still teaser, each its own edit tuned to its length and to the priority claims rather than the same file simply trimmed down. The master must be the longest and the teaser the shortest; do not hand us a 'cutdown' longer than the master. Give us the teaser as a same-length vertical 9:16 version for social, and one clean poster frame off the master for a social end-card.

B. STILLS — one look, five frames. The five stills were shot on two different days under different light, so straight out of the folder they do not match — different frames carry different color casts and exposures, and not all are perfectly straight. We want the whole set to read as ONE room in the calm, premium DARK-MODE look our brand lives in: a single shared white point with every frame sitting truly neutral, and the dark surrounds resolved to one common near-black that is deep and rich but NOT crushed to pure black and never clips a channel to zero, so the teal UI accents read cleanly against the charcoal. Use the 18% grey card each frame carries as your neutral reference and reconcile the whole set to it. On the dark-mode beauty shot we also want the console's UI to sit bright and vivid — the screen should glow against the surrounding dark without that surrounding dark itself going milky or grey. Deliver two things for this set: the matched frames as full-frame masters with the reference card still in shot so we can confirm the match, plus card-cropped versions sized for the feature cards. And tell us the white-balance (temperature / tint), exposure, and black-point settings you landed on for each of the five, so we can confirm the set was matched to one target rather than eyeballed frame by frame.

C. LOGO. We gave you the mark two ways on purpose. Get us a razor-sharp vector SVG of the logo for the end-card and corner bug, and a clean transparent-background PNG bug for the app sticker — choose the right source copy for each. The mark has an interlocking-mesh shield with real see-through gaps between the strands: those gaps must stay see-through in the transparent bug, not get filled in.

D. FEATURE CARDS. Using our authored InDesign template and the messaging matrix, produce one press-ready feature card per priority claim: bind the claim, proof point and call-to-action verbatim from the matrix, place that claim's matching graded still in the card's image frame, and the vector logo in the masthead. Hand back one press-ready ~300 DPI card per row of the matrix — do not rewrite our copy. Acceptance: every grey card reads neutral and the set is matched to one white point on one common near-black floor; the beauty shot's UI glows against an intact dark surround; the vector mark is crisp with its mesh gaps open and the photographed bug sits on clean transparency; the master is the longest video and the teaser the shortest, with the 9:16 the same length as the teaser; and there is exactly one finished card per messaging row. Two rounds of feedback should be plenty.

</details>

<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

Velvet Hour is a monthly intimate live-music night. Every month we film one acoustic set in one long, continuous single-camera take for our socials (Instagram, Facebook, YouTube) and we print a one-page-per-artist lineup sheet for the door and for the next month's promo. We are NOT reshooting anything and we do NOT want a fancy motion-graphics edit — our house style is clean, coherent, performance-first, no gimmicks. Here is the whole job, in three parts.

PART 1 - the social cut. From last month's raw footage - one long, continuous, several-minutes-long single-camera take that runs the whole stripped-back set on a locked wide of the little stage - give us one short, punchy social sizzle reel that captures the feel of the night, plus a vertical 9:16 version of that same reel for stories. Same length is fine for the vertical - just reframed so the performer stays in shot. Also pull one strong still frame out of the footage that we can treat as a gig-night poster image (see the look in Part 2).

PART 2 - the artist promos, matched then treated. Next month's lineup is four acts and their promo photos were sent in by four different people, shot on different days under whatever light they had, so straight out of the folder they read like four separate shoots. Every photographer left a standard 18% grey reference card at the edge of the frame. First, bring all four to one consistent look: neutralise each photo to the grey card it carries so that card reads truly neutral and the four sit at one shared white point and brightness - a viewer scrolling the lineup should not be able to tell they were shot by four different people on four different days. Judge every frame on its own in-frame grey card and land it on that shared target; then TELL US the white-balance and exposure move you settled on for each one so we can see the set was matched, not eyeballed. Hand back BOTH the neutralised full frames with the grey card still in shot (keep those as our proof-of-match masters so we can confirm each card really reads neutral and the four match) AND the same frames cropped to web thumbnails with the card removed. Then, on top of the matched set, give the four our signature Velvet Hour poster look: a single-hue duotone (a deep tonal treatment in one house colour, dark and moody but never crushed to dead black, punchy contrast, all four sitting at ONE matched density so the printed lineup reads as one series). The poster look has to be built as a deliberate tonal grade, not a one-click filter, and all four have to land at one shared density. Give us the four duotone posters too.

PART 3 - the mark and the printed listing. Our venue mark only exists as a flat scan on off-white paper, a little crooked, with a margin around it - clean it up and vectorise it razor-sharp for the listing masthead: straighten it, knock the paper ground off the OUTSIDE of the lettering, and set it into the pale masthead of the listing sheet (that is the only place it needs to go on this job). Finally, build the lineup sheet: we have hand-built the InDesign listing template with the real placeholder fields and two image slots (one for the artist's poster, one in the masthead for our venue mark), and we are sending the lineup data file; merge them so every artist gets their own single page with their duotone poster placed, our venue mark in the masthead, and their name, genre, set date, set time and one-line blurb set in type, and hand back a press-ready PDF - one page per artist, four artists, four pages. Bind our copy verbatim from the data file; do not rewrite it. Acceptance: every grey card neutral and the four matched to one white point (with your per-photo moves reported); the four duotone posters at one shared density (deep but nothing clipped to pure black); the mark a clean, skew-free vector with the paper knocked off the OUTSIDE of the lettering, sitting cleanly in the pale listing masthead; and exactly one finished listing page per lineup row.

</details>

<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

Lunara Silver is a growing D2C brand of handcrafted sterling-silver jewellery, and we are launching our 'Moonlit' pendant. We are NOT reshooting and we do NOT need a finished edited film here — our in-house editor cuts the hero film in Premiere. What we need from you is the production pack built off the ONE take we already have.

Here is what you are given: (1) moonlit_take_4k.mp4 — a single continuous ~40 second 4K (3840x2160) studio take, hand-held-steady, of the pendant being lifted off the linen, slowly turned so the polished silver catches the window light, a macro pass on the engraved crescent, and finally clasped and settled on the neck. Because it is one long take by a window, the light changes across it — a cloud passes partway through, and the hand shadows the piece on the macro move — so different moments in the take do NOT match each other straight out of the file: some beats are warm and bright, others go cool and dim. To make the match checkable we clipped a photographic 18% grey card onto the linen at the edge of frame, and it stays in shot the whole take. (2) lunara_shotboard_template.indd — the InDesign shot-board page we hand-built, one shot per page, with the real placeholder fields and two image slots (the shot frame and the masthead). (3) moonlit_shotlist.csv — our eight-beat shot list: the beat name, a camera note, the approximate timecode in the take, and the format tag for each of the eight shots we want on the board. (4) lunara_wordmark_flat.png — our flat wordmark on transparency, which we want razor-sharp on the board masthead.

What I need back:
- THE SHOT-BOARD (the main deliverable): a press-ready ~300 DPI PDF of our lookbook production board, ONE shot per page, eight pages, that our packaging vendor prints and pins up. For each of the eight beats on the shot list, pull the strongest, SHARP frame near that beat's timecode out of the take (if the exact timecode lands on a motion-blurred transition, step to the clean frame beside it — a soft frame prints muddy and we will reject it), grade it, and drop it into the page's shot window with its beat name, camera note, timecode and format tag bound in from the list, and our wordmark crisp in the masthead.
- THE GRADE (this is the whole craft of it): the board has to read as ONE continuous piece, not eight stills from eight different shoots. Bring every pulled frame to the SAME house look — a clean, true-to-silver grade where the neutral grey card in that frame lands truly neutral (no residual warm or cool cast) at one common white point, and the set shares one exposure feel. Because the take's light drifts, no two beats start from the same cast or brightness, so getting all eight onto that one white point is a per-frame decision — each frame has to be neutralized to its OWN in-frame grey card, and how far and which way to move is yours to judge from that card, frame by frame. A set that is each 'auto-fixed' to look fine on its own will drift apart at the grey cards and we will reject it. Keep the silver reading like real metal — bright, not blown; neutral, not blue. When you are done, hand back, per frame, the white-balance (temperature / tint) and exposure move you dialed and the final pixel size, so we can confirm the board was matched to one target rather than eyeballed frame by frame.
- PRINT SIZE: each board page drops the frame into a 130 x 173 mm portrait shot window, and at press resolution that window needs at least ~1535 x 2044 px of real image. The take is 4K, so a portrait crop taken from the FULL frame just clears that; a frame you graded on a small proxy, or a landscape frame stretched to fill a portrait window, will fall under and print soft — do not enlarge past what the 4K frame actually holds.
- THE TEASER: a full-length 9:16 vertical (1080x1920) reframe of the whole take for the launch-announcement story — same runtime, reframed to vertical, no trimming and no upscaling (the 4K master has the height for it).
- THE WORDMARK: our flat wordmark cleaned to a crisp SVG for the board masthead and reusable on future covers.

Keep the sources in our Creative Cloud folder. Bind the beat names, camera notes and timecodes verbatim from the shot list — do not rename our beats. Acceptance: every grey card neutral and the eight pages matched to one white point with the per-frame moves reported; every board frame at least ~1535 x 2044 px so it prints >=300 DPI in the 130 x 173 mm window; the teaser exactly 1080x1920 at the take's full runtime; the wordmark crisp vector on every masthead; and exactly one board page per shot-list row.

</details>

<details><summary>Full client brief — paste THIS to the solver</summary>

NOURA is a direct-to-consumer wellness brand — a daily greens + adaptogen powder that (in our words) 'actually tastes like something you'd drink on purpose.' We run paid social on TikTok, Instagram Reels, Meta feed and YouTube, and we're scaling our UGC ad program. For this assignment we're handing over a batch of raw creator footage and want it cut into a short-form ad package we can put straight into ad sets and A/B test.

What we're sending: (a) three raw vertical UGC talking-head clips from three different creators — a kitchen 'morning routine' take, a bathroom-mirror 'get ready with me' take, and a post-workout porch take — all shot on phones, ungraded and flat; (b) one product b-roll clip — the powder being scooped into water, stirred, condensation on the glass, the tub and a single-serve sachet on a marble counter; (c) our wordmark logo as a flat PNG; (d) a photoreal hero still of a creator holding the tub, straight off the phone (flat, dull white balance), to become the ad thumbnail / cover; (e) a brand color-reference frame representing the bright, sunny, fresh-green look we grade toward; (f) a hooks CSV listing the different opening hooks / angles / CTAs we want to test; (g) a caption-cue JSON for the on-screen captions; and (h) a brand-kit note with our colors, fonts, tone, and a compliance line (structure/function language only — NO disease or medical claims on any asset).

Deliverables we need, mapped to Adobe Creative Cloud connector tools with every step honestly tagged for execution mode:

A. VIDEO — (1) probe the raw clips so we know resolution / frame rate / duration before cutting; (2) summarize the footage + b-roll so we agree on the strongest visual moments and a logical flow, steered by our hooks CSV; (3) produce the primary deliverable — one polished ~17s UGC MASHUP master that weaves all three creators + b-roll around Hook A; (4) produce two tighter hook-variant reels as their own passes — an ~17s Hook B 'skeptic-turned-believer' cut and a ~15s Hook C 'results' cut (repurposed from the same footage, NOT exact-timestamp trims); (5) reframe: the master to 16:9 (YouTube / VSL) and 1:1 (feed), and each hook-variant reel to ~17s (TikTok / Reels / Shorts) — same length, no trimming.

B. THUMBNAIL / COVER — from the flat hero still, build a scroll-stopping graded ~17s cover: auto-tone baseline, push the bright warm brand color temperature toward our reference, shape the fresh-green + warm-skin HSL, select and pop the creator/product subject, lift the highlights for the airy look, and crop clean to 1080x1920.

C. ON-BRAND TEXT / GRAPHIC PLATES (standalone PNG / SVG references, NOT composited onto the video) — recommend an on-brand caption typeface; vectorize the wordmark to a clean SVG for the end-card and corner bug; build an opaque lower-third caption-bar plate and an opaque callout-badge plate by selecting a region on the graded canvas and solid-filling it with brand color (position/color references the editor rebuilds on the timeline); and a graded end-card the ads close on. Captions themselves ship as the supplied caption-cue sheet.

D. PACKAGING — copy all the cuts + reframes, the thumbnail, the end-card, the logo SVG, the plates, and the caption sheet into one dated handoff folder and give us a share link.

Heads-up we already understand: frame-accurate timeline cuts, animated motion graphics, burned-in captions/text, and hard transitions are a manual Premiere / After Effects finish and are OUT of scope for the automated connector pass. The automated pass delivers the AI mashup + hook variants, the reframes, the graded thumbnail and end-card, the vector logo, the caption/callout plates, and the caption sheet — the human editor does the final timeline polish, burns the captions/callouts using the plates, and locks the logo on top. Fast turnaround, lean budget — efficient workflow over flashy effects.

</details>

Lean budget, quick turnaround.

What we need done, mapped to Adobe Creative Cloud connector tools with every step honestly tagged for execution mode:

A. VIDEO — (1) summarise the four raw clips so we agree on the strongest moments and the sizzle order before cutting; (2) produce the master: one fast ~17s AI sizzle cut of the four clips, steered toward warm, appetising, high-energy pacing; (3) reframe that master to a 9:16 vertical reel and a 1:1 square, each SAME length (a reframe, not a re-trim); (4) QC the vertical reel's dimensions / duration / codec before handoff. NOTE up front: the actual warm colour grade on the moving footage is a manual Premiere/Lumetri finish and is OUT OF SCOPE for the automated connector pass — the connector delivers the sizzle assembly, the reframes and everything below.

B. HERO COVER / THUMBNAIL + THE WARM LOOK — from the flat plated-hero still, build the warm, appetising cover the reel opens on and that also locks the look the editor grades the footage toward: auto-tone baseline, push the white balance warm/golden, lift the highlights so the food glistens, boost the warm red/orange food tones, add overall vibrance, then select just the plated dish and pop it against the background, lay a subtle warm ember wash over the whole frame, and crop clean to a 1080x1350 portrait cover.
